By the blessed Mar Ephrem. The first.
Against False Teachings.

Ephrem to Hypatius, my brother in our Lord: greetings.... May our peace toward everyone increase, and may peace between us grow. May we be established in the peace of truth, and may we make still greater use of the greeting of a letter. Here I am, willingly writing what I had not wanted to write. For I had not wanted a letter to serve as the means of communication between us, since it can neither ask questions nor be questioned. Instead, I wanted speech that can ask questions and be questioned to serve as the means of communication between us. I wanted communication from mouth to ear. A written sheet is like a body made up of parts, just as a tongue that acts freely is like a mind that acts freely. For a body cannot add to or subtract from the measure of its stature; neither can a sheet add to or subtract from the measure of its writing. Spoken words, however, can remain within a measure or go beyond it. For the Godhead gave us speech that acts freely, like itself, so that speech that acts freely might serve our freedom to act. Through speech we have also become the likeness of its giver, since through it we have the impulse to consider good things and reflect upon them. And not only good things: through speech, the gift that comes from him, we also come to know God himself, the source of good things. For through this, which resembles God, we are clothed in God's likeness. Divine teaching is a stamp for minds, by which people who learn are stamped, so that they may become an image of the one who knows everything. For if Adam became God's image through his authority, it is far more glorious when a person becomes God's image through knowledge of the truth and truthful conduct. For authority itself also rests upon these things. Animals cannot form within themselves a clear conception of God, because they have no speech, which is precisely what depicts the image of truth within us. We have received the gift of speech, not so that we should behave like animals that cannot speak, but so that in our actions we should resemble God, the giver of speech. How great speech is! It is a gift that came to make those who receive it like its giver. And because animals have no speech, they cannot even become a likeness of our mind. But because the mind possesses speech, it is a great disgrace to it whenever it is not clothed in God's likeness. The disgrace is still more severe when animals become like human beings, while human beings do not become like God. Thirdly, the punishment is doubled whenever this intermediate being abandons the good that is above him, and descends from the rank of his nature to clothe himself, through his conduct, in the likeness of animals. A letter, then, cannot

give a satisfactory answer about everything someone wants to ask, because a letter’s tongue is far away from it, since its tongue belongs to its writer. Even when a letter speaks what is written in it, it borrows another tongue for itself, so that the letter may speak through it. Though it is silent, it speaks through two silent tongues: one is the pen with its ink, and the other is the sight of the eye. But if we rejoice so much in a letter poor in treasures, how much more will we rejoice in a tongue close at hand, which has authority and is the keeper of the inner treasures! I wished that, instead of seeing me in the figures on the paper, you could see me in the features of my face. And instead of the written words of my letter looking at you, I wished that my eyes could see you in place of my written words. But because the sight of our faces is not worthy of the chaste gaze of your eyes, you are looking instead at the figures in our letter. Pure writings, then, have fittingly been set before your pure eyes. I am not saying that what is pure is defiled by what is unclean, but that someone who is not pure is not worthy to be looked upon by pure eyes. For even though the people had thoroughly sanctified their bodies for three days, because they had not sanctified their hearts, he did not allow them to approach the holy mountain. It was not because holiness itself would be defiled by the unclean, but because those who were unclean were not worthy to approach holiness. But through holy Moses, who went up the holy mountain, God gave an example to encourage the pure and rebuke the unclean: all those who are holy like Moses are close to holiness like Moses. For whenever one of the body’s members is given rest, all the members receive a pledge of rest, because they too, together with that one member, will be given rest like it. For in the body in which our Lord rose from the dead, all bodies received a pledge that they too, together with him, would rise like him. As for your urging my humble self, my brothers, to come to you, know that if I had wanted to, I could have come. But know also that if I could have come, I would not have wanted to be deprived of it. For I could have come, because I had decided to. In simplicity, I could have come out of love. But with discernment, I could not come because of fear. Whoever becomes childishly drunk with love rises above fear. But whoever lies trembling beneath fear is constantly lashed by groundless dread. He also helped the athletes in the contest to rise above fear through the encouragement of good hope. And not to fall under the debilitating anxiety that a frightened mind conjures up. Yet perhaps athletes have good reason to be afraid. For the winner is crowned, and the loser is disgraced. Victory is not divided between the two of them. But we had no need to fear a contest in which defeat was victory. For when the teacher wins distinction, the learner too is greatly helped. For both the one who helps and the one who is helped share in the benefit. For if we had come to teach, it would have been a victory for everyone, since my error would have been stifled by our truth. But if we could not teach, yet could learn, it would have been a victory—a victory for everyone. For through your knowledge, ignorance would have been abolished. The treasury of the one who enriches everyone stands open before everyone. Grace attends to it, never withholding anything from those who ask for discernment. If, then, we had anything, we could have given as givers; and if we had nothing, we could have received as those who ask. But even if we could neither give nor receive, our coming could not have been empty of every good thing. For even if we could not examine you with our minds, we could have seen you with our eyes. And we had no greater gift than seeing you. Moses bears witness to this. For although he was granted the power to do everything like God, in the end he left everything behind and begged to see the Lord of everything himself. For if the Creator’s creatures are so desirable to look at, how much more desirable to look at is their Creator! But because we have no eye capable of looking at his radiance, we have been given a mind capable of contemplating his beauty. A person, then, is greater than his possessions, just as God is greater and more beautiful than his creatures. But know, my beloved, that if we had come, it could not have been the case that we were entirely needy people who receive everything, nor, in turn, that you were perfect givers who give everything. The one who lacks something does not lack everything, so that he may not be put to shame; nor is the one who is accomplished accomplished in everything, so that he may not become proud. This deficiency came about so that completeness might be born from it. For because we need to give to one another and receive from one another, the deficiencies of us all are filled by the resources of us all. For just as the deficiencies of the body’s members are supplied by one another: In the same way, the inhabitants of the world meet the common need out of the common abundance. Let us therefore rejoice in the need we all share, for from it harmony is born for us all. Because people need one another, the high bend down toward the lowly without shame. And the small reach up toward the great without fear. We even care for animals because we need them. Simply put, our need for everything binds us in love for everything. O hated need, from which beloved harmony is born! Because regions need one another, their need joins them together like a body, so that, like limbs, they give to one another and receive from one another. These dependent orders belong to one rich provider, whose need is this: to give to everyone, while he himself has no need to receive from anywhere. For even what he appears to receive from us, he takes from us with loving ingenuity, so that he may return it to us many times over, as though repaying a debt. This is ingenuity in the service of good, which our cunning in the service of evil ought to imitate. Now, concerning the fear I mentioned above: the force of fear has pressed not only upon us who are weak, but also upon those who are mighty and valiant. I do not say this to find consolation for our foolishness, but to offer a reminder to your wisdom. For Peter defied fear and wanted to walk on the water. Although he went forward because his love urged him on, he nearly sank because fear came upon him. Fear, which had been weaker than he was on dry land, reached the midst of the waves, the place where it grows strong, and gained strength against him and defeated him. From this we can also learn that all the desires within us, when any one of them joins with a bad habit that supports it, then gain strength and overcome us. Fear and love were weighed as though in a balance in the midst of the sea, and fear weighed heavier and prevailed. And Simon, whose faith fell short and rose in the balance, was himself close to sinking in the sea. This too is a symbol that teaches us. Its meaning is frightening: all those whose good deeds are light and rise in the just balance are themselves close to sinking into evil. But if someone asks, “What need is there to construct comparisons like these?” let him know that there is no harm in taking from everything an illustration that helps our weakness. If, then, Peter feared the waves while the Lord of the waves was holding him by the hand, how much more will the weak fear the waves of controversy, which are far stronger than the waves of the sea! For in the waves of the sea it is bodies that drown, but in the waves of inquiry it is minds that sink or are tossed up. Again, that tax collector who was praying in the temple was also very persistent in asking for forgiveness. Because he was greatly afraid of punishment, he stood there in fear and love. He loved the Merciful One because of his forgiveness, and he feared judgment because of its retribution. And while his love led him to pray lovingly, his fear kept him from daring to raise his eyes to heaven. Although grace was running ahead to meet him, his fear could not boldly cross the boundary of righteousness. If the fear of the tax collector who was justified knew its measure and did not presume to cross the boundary, how does weakness dare to disregard its measure and cross the boundary of propriety? For this too—that a person should know the level of his weakness and not aspire to a level beyond his strength— I think such a person cannot stumble. For he does not run toward a level too difficult for him, from which he would fall. For people run without understanding toward levels too difficult for them. Before they ascend, pride drives them on; and after they fall, remorse torments them. But again, I also see that the bold persistence of which our Lord spoke was praised and enriched precisely because its boldness dared to cross the boundary of propriety. For if it had held back and observed propriety, it would have gone away empty-handed. But because it pressed on and trampled harmful shame as though beneath its heels, it received more than it had been asking for. Oh, the need whose bold cries enriched its poverty! For it did not help need to remain under harmful restraint; rather, its boldness had to become a good weapon for obtaining good things. But if bold persistence received all this praise because it opened closed doors and raised those sleeping in bed, and received more than was needed, how much blame will need deserve when it has not approached open doors or received help from the treasures of the Watchful One! Better, then, is someone who persists boldly in seeking help than someone who holds back and loses that help. For whoever observes the propriety of restraint while losing the help he needs, even the propriety he has observed stands condemned, and his propriety has become impropriety. Whoever constantly pursues exactness in his duties falls short of soundness in those duties. Wheat is excellent, but unless it sheds its coarse husk, fine flour cannot be made from it. Fruit that has not ripened is not tasty, and fruit that has ripened too much loses its flavor. When it is neither hard nor mushy, it retains its flavor. For if we go beyond proper bounds in scrutinizing things, even beautiful and clear things become distasteful. For we should act neither with ignorance nor with excessive investigation. Rather, we should use balanced, sound, and reliable discernment. For through either of the first two approaches, a person certainly slips from his path. For without knowledge, a person cannot attain knowledge. And through excessive investigation, a person cannot build on a sound foundation. For ignorance is a covering that prevents one from seeing. And investigation that constantly builds and tears down is a wheel of changes that does not know how to stop and be still. When it encounters truths in its investigation, it cannot remain with them, for its movements are confused. When it finds what it seeks, it does not value its discovery and takes no pleasure in the fruits of its labor. But if we go too far in investigating everything, we fall away from the Lord of all, because we wish to know everything as he does. Although our knowledge cannot know everything, we display an evil desire before the one who knows everything. Although he is above all in his knowledge, we who lack knowledge dare to climb to the height of his knowledge. For if we go too far in disputing things, we obscure the path of truth that we wish to follow, and confuse beautiful things through our debate—not that those beautiful things are confused by nature. It is our own weakness that becomes confused on account of great things, because we cannot fully comprehend their greatness. For there is only one who is perfect in everything, whose knowledge penetrates everything completely. We should not examine everything minutely, but should also look at things simply. Not that our knowledge should become ignorance. For even something that a person does unwisely, if he does it with wise discernment, even his lack of wisdom is wisdom. And if, through his knowledge, he becomes unknowing, so as to leave aside those things that he is unable to know, even his ignorance is great knowledge, because he knows that they cannot be known. His knowledge cannot become ignorance, for he knows well what he knows. But a mind in which many conflicting arguments arise, each undoing the other— such a mind cannot accomplish anything easily. For thoughts that conquer and are conquered are born from it. And waves that batter it from every side leave it in doubt and inactivity. It is therefore helpful for the element of simplicity in us to prevail over that of changeability. For how often the clever and subtle thoughts we have about a matter obstruct that very matter, so that it never reaches completion! Look at the activities that sustain the world: it is simplicity, without many thoughts, that brings them to completion. For these very activities succeed when a single, simple thought directs them. But amid the rush of many thoughts they come to a standstill. Farming, for example, has just one thought: namely, simply to scatter seeds in the ground. But if other thoughts intrude upon it, so that it begins to ponder or consider whether its seed will sprout or not, or whether the ground will close over it or cast it out, farming cannot sow in this way. For feeble thoughts have intruded upon one healthy thought and made it sick. And because it has become sick, it cannot accomplish anything as a healthy thought can. For health of thought, like health of body, accomplishes everything. And the farmer who cannot drive with a single ox cannot direct his work with two thoughts. Just as it is helpful to drive with two shoulders, so he ought to use one healthy thought. Even the martyrs and confessors who were crowned could not have been crowned if they had approached their struggle with two thoughts. For whenever our free will settles between keeping the commandment and breaking the commandment, it habitually seeks out two thoughts that undo each other, so that, through the interpretation offered by one, it may escape the suffering involved in the other. That is, through a deceptive outlet [?], it may throw off the burden of the commandment. And so that we do not become distracted by unnecessary things and abandon what is necessary, let us speak briefly rather than at length: whatever succeeds through one healthy thought has its health impaired by many thoughts. For if we set out to approach with elaborate devices something that we ought to approach simply, even our discernment becomes a lack of discernment. For every duty whose proper bounds a person steps beyond— All the wisdom we might apply to it is foolishness. Likewise, in any inquiry in which the inquirer strays from its truth, all the discoveries he may make, even if his discoveries are very wise, are false. For not everything that is wise is true; rather, what is true is wise. Nor is something profound merely because it is debated. Rather, what is spoken by God, when it is believed, is subtle. There is nothing so subtle as this: that everything should be done properly, according to the opportunity available for it. And if it happens that what is being done can be done simply, its very simplicity is subtlety. For it is this simplicity that we ought all the more to call subtlety, because it brings benefits to completion without elaborate arrangements and many calculations, and because it accomplishes things easily. It is this that resembles the divine nature, which creates everything easily. It is therefore the benefit of things that we ought to seek, rather than their investigation. And if their simplicity is judged by debaters, there are indeed many things that appear plainly condemned, yet their hidden reality stands in great victory. For it appears that nothing is simpler than this: that a farmer should take the gathered seeds he holds in his handfuls and scatter them in the ground. But after a time, when what was scattered is seen gathered together and coming in abundance, like a commander with his army, and the seed that was considered lost is found and has found others along with it, then one marvels at the farmer’s simplicity, which has become a fountain of wisdom. From this, then, and through it, hear also the opposite case. If someone spares the gathered seed so as not to scatter it, he certainly seems to act wisely, since he takes care not to scatter it. But when he sees the farmer’s scattered loan gathered together and repaid to him by the earth with principal and interest, then that apparent discernment, which took care not to scatter, is seen to be blindness, because it was deprived of gathering a harvest. It does not help us, then, to be constantly misled by names, nor to be deceived by outward appearances. For if it was because I wisely decided, “I ought not to venture to come,” that I did not come, perhaps it would have benefited me not to have decided wisely. For perhaps my coming to you would have succeeded in a childlike and simple way. But know this too: if I were coming thoughtlessly, I would not want to come, because our coming would have been without discernment. For we would have had no fruit of understanding. For everything done without discernment comes either from unthinking habit or from blind activity. It has no root in the minds of those who do it. But if both these choices are conscious, both coming and not coming belong to my will. This is the single will, one half of which is fighting against its other half. And when it conquers and is conquered, it is crowned in both. This is a wonder: although the will itself is one, two unequal inclinations are found within its unity. I know that what I have said is so. But I do not know how to explain why. For I marvel at how a single thing both subjects something to itself and is itself subjected by that same thing. But know that if this were not so, human beings would have no freedom to govern themselves. For if our willing is compelled, we have no freedom. And again, if our will itself is bound and cannot either will or refrain from willing, we have no power over ourselves. Therefore, this must be required: that there should be a single thing which, although it is one, can easily become two whenever this one thing wishes. And whenever it wishes, it can also easily become one or many. For in a single day, ten thousand desires that undo one another are born within us. This is the will, the root that gives them birth, which is both one and many. This is the will that produces sweet and bitter fruits. O free root, master of its own fruit! If it wishes, it makes its fruits bitter, and if it wishes, it makes its produce sweet. For God, for whom nothing is difficult, created within us something that is difficult for us to describe: the self-governing will. Although it is one, it has two inclinations: both to will and not to will. When it has fought and one half of it has conquered the other half, then the whole will be crowned by the whole. For this is an indescribable wonder: although the will is one, how can one half of it rebel against the law, while the other half is subject to the law? For there are two inclinations within it that contend with one another. For one part of the will desires that evil should be done, while another part restrains it and takes care that it should not be done. And how is it that the will itself has not been changed by that part of it which desires evil things, so as to become like that evil-desiring part, nor has it been transformed so as to become entirely good, like that part of it which loves good things? But if both these parts can turn toward good and toward evil, what, then, should we call them? Those we call evil can become good, and those we call beautiful can become ugly. And although both can become one thing, unless they divide again and become two, there can be no contest. It is a marvel that we cannot express, yet neither can we remain silent about it. For we know that there is one will within us, with many distinctions. But although the root is one, we do not understand how half its taste is sweet and half bitter, even though it is not entirely hidden from us. Nor do we understand how that bitterness is absorbed into the sweetness and becomes pleasant like it, or how, again, once the sweetness has been absorbed, it mingles with the bitterness and becomes bitter like it. And how, again, when these two dispositions have been absorbed into one another and have become one thing in friendship, they separate from one another again and stand opposed to one another in hostility. For where was that disposition which makes us repent after sins, before the sins? And how did that disposition which was frenzied before adultery become repentant after adultery? These are the dispositions that act like leaven upon one another, changing one another and being changed by one another. Here, however, our truth has defeated the doctrines and bound them so that not one of them can stand up in debate. But if anyone from these schools of teaching wishes to debate, let him know that we have now been called not to fight with enemies, but to converse with friends. But when the conversation between friends is finished, then our truth too will demonstrate its strength in the contest. These things I have said are easy for everyone to recognize, because there are two dispositions in everyone, set against one another in a contest. Between them stands the divine law, holding a crown and a punishment, so that when there is victory it may offer the crown, and when defeat appears it may impose punishment. But if the evil within us is evil and cannot become good, and likewise the good within us is good and cannot become evil, then these promises of good and evil that the law makes are superfluous. For whom would the giver of rewards crown? Someone who is victorious by nature and cannot be defeated? Or whom, again, would the one who exacts punishment condemn? A nature that is defeated and cannot win? But if that good thing within us itself obeys what is evil, how can we call it good? For look, it has a close kinship with evil. For its kinship with evil is revealed in the very fact that it obeys evil. For evil itself could not have drawn it toward itself unless its composition were akin to evil’s leaven. See, then, that even what they call the good nature is itself exposed, by its own self, as an evil nature, because it has an evil will that is drawn after evil. But by this very fact that it has an evil will, it has attached all evils to itself. For nothing is worse than an evil will, since it is the root of all evils. For whenever there is no evil exercise of free will, these evils too cease. For even a deadly sword cannot kill without the evil will of the person holding it. But look, already, while we have not yet approached the battle itself, before the battle, the enemies of truth have been defeated in advance. And if someone asks, “What, then, is this will?” we can tell him, “This is precisely what it truly is: self-governing freedom.” And because we should not treat a good student with contempt, we should not now toss him a word like people hurrying past. This, however, is one of truth’s sayings. For in a sound and wise listener, even from a single word of truth, a great faith comes to life within him, just as a great flame is born from a small ember. For if one of fire’s small embers is powerful enough to leave marks on the body, then even one of truth’s words is not too weak to cleanse the stains of error from the soul. So, to the person who asks, “What is this will, then, since, although it is one, part of it is good and part of it evil?” we shall say, “Because it is will.” And if he goes on asking, we shall tell him, “Because it has authority over itself.” And if he keeps on arguing further, we shall tell him, “Because it is freedom.” And if he is not persuaded, his very refusal to be persuaded demonstrates that, because he has freedom, he does not wish to be persuaded. But if he is persuaded when they tell him that there is no freedom, this is the wonder: his freedom has been persuaded by the denial of his freedom. This, however, puts an end to his hope. The matter resembles a speaker who wishes to deny, and to persuade others, that human beings have no speech. And it is great madness that, while using speech, he says that there is no speech. For his own speech refutes him. For by that very argument he tries to prove that argument does not exist. So too, when free will sets out to hide itself in debate, and to demonstrate by persuasion that it does not exist, then its existence is all the more clearly detected and seen. For if there were no free will, there would be no debate or persuasion. But if, when it hides itself, it becomes all the more visible, and when it denies itself, it is all the more exposed, then whenever it reveals itself, it appears as clearly as the sun. Why, indeed, does free will wish to deny its authority and acknowledge slavery, when no yoke of mastery has been laid upon it? For it does not belong to the race of crawling creatures that are in subjection, nor to the kind of beasts that are enslaved, but to the lineage of the king and the king’s children, who alone among all creatures were created in the image of God. Indeed, everyone is ashamed of the name of slavery and even denies it. If a slave goes to a place where people do not know him and becomes rich there, though he is a slave and descended from slaves, he may even feel compelled to say there that he comes from a family of free people and from royal stock. This is the astonishing thing: slaves deny their slavery, while the free will of fools denies its own existence. Notice that if people call the man who says there is no free will a slave, he takes offense and becomes angry. He begins to demonstrate the free status of his family. How is it that on one side he denies freedom, while on the other he acknowledges it? On one side he hates visible slavery, yet he acknowledges hidden slavery. If he chose discerningly and weighed the matter soundly, he would not acknowledge that very slavery, lest he be deprived of the mind’s sovereign freedom. Here he is exposed as having blasphemed most wickedly against the Good One, the giver of free will, who subjected the earth and everything in it to its authority. But no one who has entered a hard contest and won a crown through great toil says that there is no free will, lest he lose the reward of his toil and the praise for his crown. It is the one who has been defeated who says there is no free will, so that he may conceal the evil guilt of his weak will. If you see someone saying that there is no free will, know that he has not exercised his free will well. But a sinner who acknowledges that free will exists may receive mercy because he has acknowledged that his offenses are his own. But the person who denies this, saying that there is no free will, is a great blasphemer, who hastens to pin his vile deeds on God. He seeks to free himself from accusation, and Satan from blame, so that all the guilt may be left with God. Far be it! May this never happen! But if he is discerning, he should not suppose that someone who has authority over himself is like a prisoner bound by his nature. Nor should he, after hearing about the will, have gone on to ask what the will is. Or does he really know everything, when he cannot even know this? But if he knows what a nature bound by necessity is, he can know what a will with power over itself is. Yet what has power over itself cannot be without that power, because it has power over itself. But in what does this power consist, if not in its ability to will and not to will? For if so, he does not wish to be persuaded, because the power of freedom is great. Our mouth cannot do it full justice. Our weak mouth has admitted that it cannot describe freedom’s self-governing will. For it is freedom that, because of its power over itself, has placed even God under investigation and accusation. It dared to raise all this, because it wished to speak about the one who cannot be expressed in words. Yet the very freedom that dared to speak about God cannot give a complete account of itself. But concerning this too, we say to the person who asks that this is the marvel: it is very easy to perceive it, but very difficult to explain it. Nor is this alone like that; everything else is like that too. For everything that exists can be discussed without being fathomed. It is possible to know that it exists, but it is not possible to fathom how it exists. For see: we can perceive everything, but we cannot fully fathom anything. We perceive great things, but cannot fully fathom even insignificant things. Give thanks, then, to the one who has granted us knowledge of the visible aspects of things, so that we may learn how much we excel. But he has not granted us knowledge of their hidden aspects, so that we may realize how deficient we are. Thus he has granted us both to know and not to know, so that our immaturity may be nurtured by the things that can be known, and through the things that cannot be known, our presumption may be restrained. Thus it was not in order to make us ignorant that he withheld knowledge from us, but so that our ignorance might be a fence around our knowledge. For see: we wish to know even the height of heaven and the breadth of the earth, but we cannot know them. And through this very inability to know, we can be restrained from toiling at it. Thus our ignorance has proved to be a boundary for our knowledge, and our lack of learning has in turn checked the impetuosity of our presumption. For when someone knows that he cannot measure a spring of water, this very inability keeps him from trying to drain what cannot be drained. Through this experience, our weakness has been shown to be a wall against our presumption. Likewise, when we know that we cannot know, then we stop investigating. For if, while knowing little, we have taken on the impetuosity of presumption, And he went out toward things that cannot be known. Who would not give thanks to the one who spared us this exhausting struggle? Even though we are unwilling to remain within the proper boundary in which he has placed us. Our ignorance, then, serves as a bridle for our knowledge. From these testimonies it is clear that the one who knows everything did not wish to make us ignorant. Rather, he placed our knowledge inside a protective enclosure that helps us. A little knowledge that recognizes its own smallness—that it does not know—is better than great knowledge that does not recognize its own limits. And a weak person who carries what is needed for his life is better than a strong, conceited person who wears himself out with lofty things that bring about his destruction. Now this is the beginning of our knowledge: to know that we know nothing. For if we know that we do not know, then through our knowledge we overcome error. For when we know that everything that exists is both known and not known, through this very understanding we acquire true knowledge. For whoever supposes that he can know everything is deprived of knowledge of everything. For through his knowledge he has gained ignorance for himself. But whoever knows that he cannot know is the one for whom knowledge has been born out of ignorance. For by knowing that he cannot know, he has, through this very thing, become able to know. This is what has helped him. Now, if, as I said above, the will is one, yet one half exercises compulsion and the other half is compelled, by whom, then, was I compelled not to come, if not by my own will? If only an alien compulsion from outside had risen against me! Perhaps then my whole self would have fought against the whole of it and prevailed. But instead, a compulsion from within has risen against me, one that I do not even know how to describe. For I do not know how to explain how one half of me fights against the other half. And through myself and within myself, I am constantly both victorious and defeated. But we are not speaking as the heresies speak. For they say that the substances of good and evil are mingled within us, and that it is these substances themselves, they claim, that overcome and are overcome by one another. But even if error has managed to adorn the counterfeit, the furnace of truth can expose it. For we say that it is the choices of free will themselves that overcome and are overcome by one another. For this is free will: that which the voice of the law can change. And if they say, “If free will comes from God, then the impulses toward good and evil that arise in it also come from God,” what exactly do they mean by saying this? Perhaps that there is no free will? And if they deny free will, what can they affirm? For if they deny free will, law and teaching are rendered useless. Let the books and laws, then, be rolled up. Let the judges rise from their seats and stop teaching. Let the prophets and apostles be questioned about their teachings: why they labored [?] to preach, or why the Lord of them all himself came into the world. But if they acknowledge it, it is by free will that they acknowledge it. The free will they acknowledge compels them to deny the evil they have acknowledged, for the two cannot both stand. Either it is our will that sins and is also justified, and this is why we have free will; or, if it is the temperaments of good and evil that are active within a person, then it is temperament that prevails and is overcome, not the will. But if someone says that whatever stirs within our free will does not belong to free will, he is using his free will to speak against free will. For how can he call it free will when he turns around and binds it by saying that it is not free? For the name of freedom stands on its own: it is free, not enslaved; independent, not subject; unbound, not bound; will, not nature. And just as, when someone calls fire by its name, its heat is made known, and the coldness of snow is understood from its name, so the power of free will is also perceived in its name. But if someone says that the impulses active within free will do not belong to it, he wants to call constrained nature free will, although this name does not fit nature. He is thus found not to understand what free will is. He uses its name carelessly and foolishly, while refusing to acknowledge its power. Either let him deny it—and see, he is refuted by its activity—or, if he acknowledges it, his own senses are fighting one another, since he denies with his mouth what he acknowledges with his tongue. For the giver of free will is not confused like this man, whose one half is divided against the other, so that he should turn around and quarrel with himself: giving us free will that receives impulses toward good and evil from him, and then turning around and laying down a law for it, so that it should not openly do the evil things that secretly stir within it from him. Let us ask a little further: when it was possible for him to give us free will, was he unwilling to give it, although he was able to give it? Or was it impossible for him to give it, and was that why he could not give it? And if he could not give free will, how could he give a law when there was no free will? But if he gave a law, the justice in his law reproves our free will, for he repays it according to its deeds. And if there is no free will, does not this charge that he brings against us concerning free will indeed testify that we have free will? For nature, being constrained, cannot express all these variations in argument. For if all human beings uniformly said the same thing, or did the same thing, there might be room for us to make the mistake of thinking that there is no free will. But if even a single person— in a single day his free will turns through many changes, so that he becomes good or evil, ugly or beautiful, merciful or merciless, bitter or pleasant, a giver of blessings or accursed, grateful or ungrateful, resembling God or Satan—with ten thousand times ten thousand witnesses, will you not then admit that we have free will? For look, every matter is established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. Examine all these variations that I mentioned above, and see that they are not found in any of the constrained natures: neither in the sea nor on dry land, neither in the heavenly lights nor in the stars, neither in trees nor in roots, nor even in animals— for animals have sensation too—nor even in birds, which have sight and hearing. Rather, if hawks are predatory, they are all predatory; and if wolves are destructive, they all do harm. And if lambs are innocent, they are all harmless; and if snakes are cunning, craftiness belongs to them all. But a human being, through his free will, can resemble them all, whereas they cannot resemble him. That is why they have nature, while we have free will. You have said “freedom”: learn its authority from its name. And you have said “slavery”: learn its subjection from its name. And you have said “nature”: recognize its constraint from its name. And you have said “God”: recognize his existence from his name. For these are names whose truth is not disputed. If you have named these things willingly, you have necessarily acknowledged them for yourself, even unwillingly. Deny free will! From this very denial and through it, we can recognize how powerful free will is, since by its own authority it has fought against its own authority. For even this very act of someone saying that there is no free will— it is because he has free will that he has been able to say that there is no free will. And so, however ingeniously free will devises every sort of variation, those very variations proclaim to us that it exists. For nature, being constrained, cannot change. Why, then, do we need testimony from elsewhere as to whether free will exists or does not exist? For look, the testimony about it is proclaimed from itself and through itself. For when it denies that it has authority over itself, it is exposed as not being subject to another either. For whoever acknowledges that free will exists ought not to bring compulsion against it. But if, as these people say, the mixtures of good and evil overcome and are overcome, they can acknowledge a mixture of good and evil. Likewise, if they deny that there is a mixture, only then can they acknowledge that there is free will. But if this is what they say—that when the mixture of evil increases, free will is forcibly driven by it— what, then, do the heretics teach in their assemblies except the error in which they themselves were trained? For if they teach, it is because there is free will; and if there is no free will, let them shut their mouths and stop teaching. But let them be asked: are they teachers of free will, or changers of our nature? Now if someone mistakenly eats a deadly root, the eater's will cannot change it. Rather, it is an evil mixture whose nature cannot be changed by words. How, then, can a just judge condemn human beings for not changing by their will an evil nature that cannot be changed by the will? Either, then, let them acknowledge that these are unfettered acts of free will that change toward good or evil, or let them acknowledge that, if they are bound natures of good and evil, natures cannot be overcome by words. For they ought to administer an antidote, like theriac against deadly bile. For it is by evidence drawn from nature that the teaching falsely constructed from analogies drawn from nature ought to be refuted. But truth is powerful enough, with a single counterstroke, to undo the many constructions of falsehood. For it is clearly evident from what I am saying that it is not the respective weights of good and evil that overcome and are overcome by one another. For look: a person can think even a hundred good thoughts in a single hour. And if good thoughts multiply in a person because goodness has greatly increased within him, look: a person can do the opposite of this in that very hour. For immediately after those good thoughts, a person can think even ten thousand evil thoughts. Which of the two, then, do they maintain was more abundant than the other? And if they say that evil was more abundant, how, when all that evil was present within the person, did it allow him to think all those good thoughts? And if evil voluntarily made room, then evil is good, since it had this good intention. For it was evil itself that, when it wished, finally overcame good. How did it consent from the beginning to be defeated by it? But if they say that there was a great abundance of good, in which of a human being’s limbs, then, did all this good hide itself and give the little evil room to rise up and display a great victory? If, then, evil was assigned to be defeated before good, that evil is better than good, since it took the crown and gave it to its opponent. But if good itself consented to give evil room to win, good is worse than evil, since it gave evil room to cause destruction. It has therefore become clear to anyone with the knowledge to understand that it is not weights and mixtures of good and evil that overcome and are overcome by one another. Rather, it is the choices of free will that conquer and are conquered, although all the choices can become a single choice. For if good choices spring up in us from that good root which is in us, and evil choices are born in us from that evil root which is in us, these are not the self-governing choices of the unrestricted freedom within us, but fixed natures governed by necessity. For if, as one of those who are in error said, clarity and turbidity were mixed together, free will would not be needed to distinguish a good choice from an evil one, but a strainer to separate the clear liquid from the sediment. For things that are physically mixed together need a separating hand to separate them, like the hand of a craftsman, which separates dross from silver by fire and separates clear liquid from sediment with a strainer. But if they say that these natures, in which [?] is mixed, have no freedom by which they might separate the turbidity from themselves, let us leave those natures for a little while. Even if we digress a little from our subject, let us go with them wherever they invite us. For truth, because of its strength, goes like a victor wherever it is led; and where an ambush is laid for it to be defeated, there it is crowned all the more. Let us therefore leave the natures that are bound and turn to minds that govern themselves. Let us consider these human beings who have freedom, to see whether their will can separate out and cast away the evil mixture within them, so that, on the evidence of the visible mixture of visible evil, we may believe that the hidden mixture of hidden evil can also be separated out. If, then, natural bile or deadly phlegm should become excessive in one of them, let them tell us: do chaste acts of free will separate out this evil? Or medicinal drugs and roots. Does not the practice itself refute them? For this natural condition of which you spoke is removed not by the righteous exercise of free will, but by the art of medicine. If, then, this small evil mixed into us is not uprooted from us by chaste conduct, but by the force of drugs, then that great and powerful evil mingled with souls— how can commandments and laws remove it? For look, as experience has taught us, even that evil they speak of—even it can be separated from us by force, through the methods of an art, and not through freely chosen conduct. For if they deny this, then let no one listen to them telling worthless tales to foolish minds. For only someone whose mind is devoid of truth believes worthless stories. If, then, murderous evil too is mingled with human beings like natural bile, let them listen with a healthy ear to a true statement: just as the vessel containing bile, when it becomes full, needs to be emptied by drugs, so that the bile does not overflow and produce pains and injuries within us, so too, when evil increases in the soul, it needs to be purged, even month by month or year by year. For just as bile increases within us from food, so, they say, evil accumulates and increases within us from things we eat. If, then, the quantity of both increases greatly within us, clearly that fullness needs purging and emptying. For blood too, when it increases within us, or phlegm, also needs to be purged. Those, then, who could not purge evil from human beings through a visible procedure now, through an invisible forgiveness, absolve human beings of their sins! But when those people's sins do not depart from them, their sins are added sevenfold to those who absolve them. For the guilt of the sins whose forgiveness they falsely guaranteed is hung around their own necks. For rabies too, although it does not depart from the dog that has gone mad, takes hold sevenfold in those bitten by the dog. The disciples, however, were commanded to shake the dust from their feet against anyone who did not receive them. But let us shake the dust of our words against those who do not accept the truth of our words. For if there is to be a reckoning for the dust of feet, How much greater will be the demand to vindicate the truth of the statement that is wronged by its hearers! But I want to know: is free will itself the cause of wrongdoing, or is evil itself the source of sins? But if it is evil, as they say, the choices of free will cannot stop up the springs of evil. How, then, is this evil subject to our will? For look: whenever we wish, we awaken it within us to harm us. Whenever we wish, we quiet it within us so that it does not hurt us. But the clear demonstration exposes their concealed teaching. For even the fever within us is not subject to our will, so that it grows stronger or subsides whenever we wish. If, then, this feeble fever is not subject to our free will, that great evil of which they speak— who can subject it to our will? If evil has subjected itself to us, there is nothing better than it, because it has subjected its great power to our weak will. But if the force of goodness has subjected evil to us, it is clear that whenever it harms us, the Good One himself sets it in motion to harm us. And so, although evil is bad because it harms us, the one who gives it free rein to destroy us is worse than it. But we are not daring to blaspheme against the Good One. Rather, through these things that seem blasphemous, though they are not blasphemous, perhaps the blasphemy of these madmen may be rebuked. For someone who is walking off the road cannot be brought back to the road unless someone goes a little way off the road after him into the wilderness. See, then, that the nature of things has not followed our will; rather, our will has followed the nature of created things, since we use them in whatever way we can and for whatever purpose we can. But if even fire does not grow cold or hot according to our will, then that evil which has an existence of its own— how is its mighty power subject to the will of created beings? But evil does not have an existence of its own, because free will has authority over itself. And fire always preserves its hot nature. But evil does not even preserve the nature of its own existence as created fire does. Even when we do not want to be burned, fire acts according to its nature, and whenever we approach it, it burns us. How, then, can the evil mixed within us, if it too has an inherently harmful nature, harm us only when our will wishes to be harmed? If we are willing, it is our will that gives it strength. The wickedness of our will is therefore stronger than the wickedness of evil. And by their own contrary argument, evil itself is found to be subject to our free will, since, however it wishes and as much as it wishes, it compels evil accordingly. They blame Satan in vain, when their own will is more hateful than Satan. But if evil can harm our free will only when our free will wishes to be harmed, it is clear that, without realizing it, they are calling free will itself evil. For fire, which burns, does not wait for free will to consent or refuse. Rather, it harms both the willing and the unwilling equally if they approach it. But if they maintain, as they say, that our will can overcome evil, let them leave the contention of debate, and let us come to a practical test. Let one of them put even the tip of his little finger into the fire. And if his will can overcome the compelling force of fire so that it does not harm him, then it is possible to believe that the harmful nature of evil can be overcome. But if fire, when it touches only our finger, torments the whole body and causes it pain, how is it that harmful evil, although it is wholly mingled with all of us, does not even harm us like powerful fire? If they say that he does not grant us the ability to overcome fire through free will, who, then, has given them authority over evil, so that they can overcome it through their free will? But if it was the other, the Good One, who granted that our free will should overcome evil, all their blasphemy clings to this very one whom they praise, for all the blame falls upon him. For if he has altered evil in such a way that it does not harm us like harmful fire, it is clear that he can also alter the harm that evil does us today so that it does not harm us. But if he cannot, our victory still stands. Let them convince us how their free will overcomes evil, when it cannot overcome fire. Whichever argument they choose for themselves, they are caught by the very one they choose. If they say that our free will cannot overcome fire because fire possesses heat by its very nature, then evil is shown not to possess freedom by nature, and that is why our will can overcome it. But if fire, although it is created and made, does not have its harmful and hot nature diminished, how can evil, which, as they say, is a self-existent entity, have the integrity of its self-existent being diminished? That things cannot even weaken one another or be mixed with one another, unless they have an affinity that allows them to receive one another. For one opposite cannot love its opposite. How, as they say, did evil desire goodness, rush toward it, and mingle with it? And how did goodness, too, become mixed with evil and love it? And when teachers and lawgivers called to her, she despised their kings and nullified their laws. Not even the drawn swords of just judges frightened her into giving up the hateful love she had for the body, which they call a murderer. She hated and disowned the good root of her nature. And she loved to bear the evil fruits of the bitter root into which she had been grafted for a whole period of time. Who, then, can conceal the saying of the Truth, who said, “There is no good tree that produces bad fruit”? For if the soul is good and comes from a good nature, how does it bear the bitter fruits of the murderous body? And again, how does the body, which they say comes from an evil nature, bear good conduct like good fruit? But you, listener, have something greater than this to hear. For look: whenever we wish, evil becomes weak within us and does not harm us. And again, in that very blink of an eye, if we wish, it becomes intense and powerful within us and kills us. Oh, what a great wonder! Or rather, oh, what great blindness! For see: when we weakened evil within us, we did not mix anything into it so that it became weak, except a good will alone. And when it revived and grew strong again, we did not mix anything into it so that it grew strong, except an evil will. But if it is our will that weakens it or makes it bitter, is it not clear even to fools that our will itself is good and evil? It is therefore free will itself that they designate by all these names for evil. And it is against this will that they speak blasphemously without realizing it. For if someone drinks diluted wine, and mixes a good will into it, can it possibly gain potency and grow strong, without his mixing wine into it? And again, if it is potent and strong, can he weaken it by will alone, without mixing water into it? Either, then, let them take their stand on mixture, or let them take their stand on will. For if it is our will that weakens evil, their claim has been refuted—that evil became mixed with goodness, and that, as they say, goodness is being purified little by little. For look, we exercise our will within ourselves every day, yet it is not purified and does not leave us. For if we will, it is purified and leaves. Perhaps, however, our will itself would have come to an end, so that we would not even have been able to will rightly. And if the will does not come to an end, neither do good and evil. When, then, did the purification and separation of the two sides take place? And if good was purified by good, so that it rose from the depth to the height, why did evil not likewise undergo a change through evil, so that it too descended into its depths? But if they insist on this mixing, the fact remains that we overcome evil by our will. And henceforth, instead of the good words they teach, they ought to distribute good portions for people to eat or drink, so that these good portions may enter them and temper the violence of evil. For words do not temper the bitterness of roots. Rather, the harshness inherent in a nature is tempered by sweetness inherent in a nature. For deeds are not overcome by words, nor are natures changed by sounds. For evil, which exists as a substance, as they say, can be driven out by good that likewise exists as a substance. For it is force that drives back force; one substance is driven back by another substance, and compulsion is overcome by compulsion. For our word cannot move a stone without a hand, nor can our will move an object without arms. And if it cannot move objects that are unresponsive and weak, how can our will move the power of great evil? For look, force is needed, not will. For light does not drive away darkness by an act of will, nor does sweetness overcome bitterness by freedom of choice. If, then, these natures, because they are natures, require powerful compulsion and not will, how is it that good and evil, if they too have fixed natures, do not likewise require force rather than freedom of choice? But if the evil mixed into bitter and deadly roots is not tempered by will, whereas this evil in human beings is overcome by freedom of choice, how, if the evil in human beings and in roots is the very same evil, is part of it overcome by compulsion and part by will? Either evil is divided against itself, or there are two evils whose essential natures are unlike one another. And if some of it—that bile found in fruits and roots—is mixed into us and accumulates in us, if evil is one, how is the portion of it within us overcome by law and commandment, while another portion is overcome by mixtures and medicines? And counsel and instruction do nothing to help with the bile in our bodies. Nor do medicines and mixtures do anything to help the evil in our souls. Here it has become clear that the bile within us is constrained by nature, and the law cannot change it. But the evil in our souls belongs to free will; medicinal roots cannot alleviate it. Although there is much to say about these things, I do not wish to go on at length, lest it appear that we win through an abundance of words rather than through the truth. For we do not win with the weapons of philosophers and orators, whose weapon is their eloquent learning. For thanks are due to him who, without the teaching of philosophy— look!—makes his teaching triumph through our childlikeness, and his truth through our simplicity.
The first discourse against deceitful teachings is finished.
Letters of Mar Ephrem to Hypatius, arranged in sections against erroneous teachings.

The second, to Hypatius, Mani, Marcion, and Bardaisan. Examine this teaching discerningly: how it is undone by itself, rebuked by itself, and exposed by its own substance, and how its condemnation comes from itself and through itself. Just as the laborers’ own words pronounced sentence against them before the owner of the vineyard, so the very words of this teaching pronounce a sentence of condemnation against them before discerning listeners. For he set a faulty beginning against a confused ending: things that contradict one another, so that it may be known that neither of them is true. For at the beginning he said that Darkness greatly desired Light—something that does not belong by nature to this visible darkness. For even this darkness that is visible to us, according to what they say, is of the same nature as the darkness that is invisible to us. Yet this darkness flees from Light as from its adversary, and does not rush toward it as toward its delight. Here is one refutation that condemns them, drawn from the nature common to all. Listen also to another refutation against them from their own book: if Darkness greatly desired Light because it brings it comfort, how can they say that Light is its adversary and will torment it in the end? And if Light is a nature desirable and pleasing to Darkness, how does bitterness for Darkness arise from this pleasant nature? For the sweetness in our world bears witness that no bitterness is tasted within it. But if that prison which torments Darkness is built from the nature of Darkness’s own realm, A nature cannot torment itself, for fire does not burn itself. And if darkness is tormented by what belongs to it, that is difficult to accept. Then neither does the Good One find rest in his own place, and the situation turns out to be reversed: Every being that exists is distressed in its own place, and is distressed in its own place, but finds rest in the place of its opposite. For if darkness in its entirety, together with its entirety, together with everything in it, is one being, uniform throughout, it cannot be an opponent to itself, just as a lion cannot be an opponent to itself. But if that prison for darkness is built from the Good One's own place, how is his delight turned into its torment? For look, it is a delightful nature that does not change. Yet he is, they say, the architect and builder of the tomb, as their account says. A certain individual, they say, whose name is Ban, has now, to his misfortune, been made a laborer on the tomb of darkness. And how can that one being, while remaining one, have part of itself building and part of itself being built, part of itself being the tomb and part of itself the ground on which it is built? For this is what we find with our own earth: everything comes from the earth, both what makes and what is made. Because it was not created from natures and beings, it can be transformed into anything, as the Maker's command ordained. But as for them, if they are all one nature and come from one good being, how can it be divided? And how, indeed, can that nature which does not suffer be cut apart? And those who are unwilling even to break bread, so that, they say, they will not hurt the light mixed into it— do they not hurt it by cutting and splitting these stones? And if it suffers when bread is broken, how much, then, does it suffer when its limbs are cut and severed? And if it is earth that has no perception, and stones that have no feeling, how, when it is one nature and one being, can part of it be rational souls and part of it mute stones? Then it is not one essence, uniform within itself, but many essences that do not resemble one another. And if it is because of silence that they feel nothing when they are cut, look, this light too shares their nature. It is silently mixed into these things. Why, then, do they not cut and sever them, since it feels nothing? But if they do not cut them so as not to cause pain, they cause it much more suffering with their teeth when they eat it, and when they imprison it in their bellies. But if the body's maker is the Evil One, as they blasphemously claim—something that, God forbid, is not so— if darkness itself contrived to construct a prison for the soul, so that it would not escape from there, It was not difficult for him to know this: that the refining furnace he had made harms him and refines the light. But if this escaped him at first, experience could now have taught him to destroy his construction and make another body—not one that separates, but one that confines; not one that refines, but one that clouds; not one that cleanses, but one that defiles; and not one that makes room for the light, but one that covers the light. If this workmanship of the body is his, his own work testifies about him that he is a wise and resourceful maker, who could have made vessels that resist the purification of the light. But if he could have done this, yet did not do so, his workmanship is enough to praise him and rebuke those who malign him. Wise physicians also confirm this, with the limbs and the pulse bearing witness for them: that the strength supplied by food passes to the body. But if the light is gradually refined and comes out, it is clear that its nature is loose and dispersed. And if the soul shares its nature, why does it not also come out with it through refinement? For its own nature must necessarily be loose, like that of the light. Why does the light come out while the soul remains? And who gave the soul this cohesion that cannot be dissolved? If it belongs to its nature, how is half of this nature held together and half not, with half loose and dispersed and half held together and gathered? For if its nature has been held together from eternity, when the children of darkness ate it—if they ate it—they could not have dissolved its nature. For just as they cannot abolish its existence so that it no longer exists, neither could they dissolve the cohesion of its being. These statements can be made without examination, but under examination they cannot stand. And if they say that the Evil One holds the soul fast within the body so that it is imprisoned, why did he not hold fast the light that is refined and comes out, so that it would not come out? And how did he hold fast a nature that cannot be held fast? For who can hold the nature of fire fast so that it cannot be divided when a lamp is lit from it? Even when fire is closely gathered together, it can be divided because its nature is not held fast. But no one can divide a ray of sunlight, because it is entirely held together throughout, in a nature that cannot be dissolved. For if the soul, which cannot be confined, was confined because it entered a body capable of being confined, why was the light, which they say is refined and comes out, not confined along with that which shares its nature and was confined there? And if the soul has knowledge because it is gathered together and held fast, it is clear that those portions that are not held fast are deaf and without knowledge, silent and without speech, and still and without movement. Here Bardaisan, Mani’s teacher, was found to have spoken craftily when he said that the soul was blended and formed from seven portions. Yet he too is refuted by these many portions that the soul gathers and collects. They increase the mixture of seven portions beyond its proper proportion. And because it does not take portions of all the mixtures from all foods in equal measure, it happens that one of the mixtures gains the upper hand and overwhelms the rest of its companions. This excess of one is a cause of disturbance to all the mixtures. From the outward body one can learn about the soul within. For when one of its mixtures predominates through an excess of one kind of food, harm reaches the whole body. The spiritual constitution of the angels bears witness that their nature admits no increase. And not only are those holy ones above this, but neither do the unclean demons admit in their nature any increase or decrease beyond what it is. Nor has the nature of the sun ever grown greater or smaller than it is. For these things, and those that resemble them, are complete beings in which the measure of their nature is always preserved. But anything that decreases or increases, grows or shrinks, diminishes or weakens, has a nature that is perishable by its creation. Yet even over those natures that do not perish, the will that made them imperishable has authority. But we have not come now to stir up Bardaisan’s mire. Mani’s filth is enough. For look, our tongue is hurrying to finish quickly and get away from him. And if these natures described above are complete, even though they were made, how much more will the self-existent being be complete in his self-existence! Yet this teaching of madmen proclaims a self-existent nature that is deficient in every respect, whose very deficiency refutes those who proclaim it. For they put together two roots in opposition, but these are properly dismantled. For what was said without knowledge is put right by sound knowledge. And whoever is clothed in contentiousness is stripped of it by the persuasion of truth. For they posited two roots in name, although on examination they are found to be many. For he introduces offspring and lines of descent that are opposed to one another. But that, although the self-existent being is one, offspring opposed to his nature should come from him— this is not pleasing to the ear of truth. For how can that nature produce something foreign to itself? This is possible for creation, which can come into being from nothing, but by no means for the bound nature of a self-existent being. Especially when he is one, and no other self-existent beings have mingled with him. He therefore posited a self-existent being who does not die, although the offspring he begets from himself are mortal. And where could mortality have sprung up in the fruit, when it is not mixed into the root from which they came? And how does an uncompounded nature beget a compounded body—those who were seized and killed? You have heard this foolishness. Come, hear something greater than it: they say that when the First Man hunted down the children of darkness, he flayed them and made this heaven from their skins. And from their dung, they say, he spread out the earth. And from their bones, they say, he also cast, raised, and piled up the mountains. His kindness is welcome, since his falsehood is plain! They say that the luminous one's mixture and mingling were within them, since they had swallowed him from the beginning. For the whole purpose of stretching them out and arranging them was that, through rain and dew, what they had swallowed might be shaken loose, and that the natures might be separated and filtered from one another. Oh, how foolish this craftsman is! But perhaps he is an apprentice who has not yet acquired experience in the craft. For if it were wine, would he not have known to make a strainer? And if it were silver and copper, would he not have known to construct a furnace? For with these implements, which mortal wisdom has devised, the dregs are easily separated from the clear wine, and the dross from the silver. But this craftsman has not gained any sense even after many years. Even through tens of thousands of experiments, he has not managed to learn what his craft requires, namely, to use these shortcuts. Instead, he made heaven into a strainer that stands idle all summer. Even in winter it does not strain every day. And in the far south it is not even slightly moistened. The basin of this filter is very poorly made: if its clear liquid descends to the earth, then its dregs are left above in heaven. This happens the wrong way around: the clear liquid descends to bodily beings, while the dregs remain with spiritual beings. As for the other things they say about snow—how it comes about and what it is— because they are filthy, they are kept under the covering of silence. They say that he also made trees into furnaces, which do not separate fruit from dust at all times, and produce from ashes; and also seeds, which do not bring life up from the earth every day. And if, as they teach, the purified substance rises from that dung of the archons, Thus the bulk of that swallowed light came out in the excrement of the rulers who had swallowed it. This is that filthy teaching which filters portions of its god out of excrement. But if, as some of them say, just as a snake has a skin that it sheds, so heaven and earth and the rest of creation came from the shed skins of the sons of darkness, let them know that the illustration they have offered stands against them. For dead shed skins cannot come from those who are immortal by nature. For the dead skin shed by a snake itself proves that the snake too is mortal. Like its skin, it too can be divided, and like its skin, it decomposes and decays. And just as the snake’s shed skin proves that its nature is subject to decay, so the shed skin of darkness also proves that darkness too, like its skin, is mortal. For whatever comes from a substance resembles it in every respect. Therefore, whether they are shed skins or their actual hides, it is all the same. But if the sons of darkness were flayed and stretched out in the air, they themselves testify that darkness, their father, is also mortal, because he is composite. Why, then, did they not flay him too at the very beginning, so that creation would have been spared his injuries? What necessity required that he be left alive? And what was the reasoning behind allowing him to remain and return once more to fight against chaste souls? And after he had made them drunk, led them astray, disgraced them, and made prostitutes, singers, and blasphemers of them, only then did that wise builder and architect think to prepare a grave and a prison for him. Instead of the prison being built over a very long time and with great labor, the sons of light should have gathered and stoned him with these very stones, and he would have been finished. But if he would not have died because his nature is immortal, this defiled teaching stands exposed in everything it says. For how did the sons of an immortal being die? And how were the sons of a spiritual being flayed? And how were beings that are not composite dissolved? They would do well to flay Mani for lying when he said that darkness was flayed, although it has neither a hide nor a skin to shed. And again, if, as they say, the moon receives the light that is filtered out and fills up over fifteen days, and goes on emptying over another fifteen days—if, in filling little by little, it perhaps resembles a cup of days [?]. Because the refiners cannot deliver it quickly, you must pour it into the vessel little by little. Or the receiving vessels that receive it do not receive it and release it quickly. Or the place into which it is poured is small. And it expands by a portion each day. And this ship of light actually takes fifteen days to empty. That other light which is being refined and ascending—where, then, does it go and remain floating until the moon is emptied? It must dissipate and be lost, for lack of a place to receive it. And darkness swallows it again. For if, when it was far away from it, darkness sucked it in at the beginning, now that it stands at the entrance to its mouth, will it not gulp it down all the more? Consider how foolish this administrator is! Instead of going, emptying itself in a single hour, and returning, as it ought, so that the first light poured out might be preserved, and this later light being refined might not be lost—look, it wears itself out going back and forth. Only after so many days does it empty itself, so that the first light is worn away and the later light is scattered. A woman is pregnant for a long time, for her child is fully formed after nine months. But when she gives birth, she delivers that child quickly, in a single hour, so that the one being born may not suffer greatly, and so that the woman giving birth may not be greatly distressed either. But the bright and nimble moon— its offspring is delivered over so many days, so that it is worn out and its offspring is distressed. And if it gives birth to one child each day, can it not even give birth to them in a single day, like a scorpion? And if it is emptying itself, let it stay there until it has emptied itself. Why does it wear itself out coming here, when it takes nothing from here during those many days? And how is it that, from eternity to eternity, this ship of light fills at the same rate, neither taking in more nor less? This management was not wise, then. For it was not arranged that, at a time when the refining increases, it should take in more—that is, that instead of filling over so many days, it should fill in five days. If their claim were true, this very thing that I have said ought to happen. For today Mani’s teaching is widespread, and it is evident that today the refining is also abundant. But a hundred years ago this teaching did not exist. And [?] did not exist. A hundred years ago, the refining of light was less than it is today. And if the refining of light was not equal then and now, how does the moon, both then and now, fill at the same rate over the same number of days? Nor was its light less then, when those who prayed were few. Nor has its brightness increased today, now that the Manichaeans have multiplied. Rather, in the time when they did not exist and now that they do exist, the moon gains nothing today from their existence, just as it suffered no loss when they did not exist. In the moon, then, which is fixed on high, which they have made a mirror for themselves, their hidden falsehood can be seen. For if, while the Manichaeans exist, it is as though they did not exist for it, the liar has been exposed by his own teaching: although he exists, he is as though he did not exist. And if they do not exist for the moon, for which they suppose they now exist all the more, still less do they exist for God, the moon’s Lord. Thus, the luminaries through which they thought they would become known expose them all the more. Does not even the evidence of a water channel convince them? It seems that those supplying it are numerous, and those receiving it hold far more. And whenever the streams increase, the rivers fill beyond their banks and rise higher than usual. And why, indeed, does the moon’s cycle last twenty-nine and a half days? Let the fraudulent teaching that hides itself behind a demonstration drawn from nature explain this. But let us strip it so that it may be seen naked of all truth. Let them tell us, then, about that half-day: why is it lacking and not complete? Does no surplus of light occur in any month, so that what is lacking from this day might be filled? But when it is deficient, it is not complete; and if there is a surplus, it still does not become complete. If it were deficient because there was too little light, it would follow that other days too would be shortened. Likewise, when the light increased, the days would increase, and they would not be found as they are. But too little light did not cause the deficiency in the moon, nor has an abundance of light filled this missing half. This very missing half-day exposes those who go astray, because they lack the whole of that truth. And because truth swiftly reproves them, as it passes from the moon to the sun, through the pair of luminaries it exposes those whose understanding has become so completely darkened while they worship the luminaries. For just as someone who worships the Lord of the luminaries is enlightened, so someone who exchanges worship of him for worship of the luminaries becomes darkened. Let us, then, state what they say, but let us not affirm it as they do. For they say that the sun receives this light from the moon. How fitting these receivers are, receiving from one another! And is there, then, no room in the sun for it to receive all these portions from the moon in a single day? But perhaps it could receive them, while the moon could not give them. Yet someone carrying a load is compelled to hurry and throw off the weight he has taken up. And how is it that, when the sun receives fifteen portions of pure light, no addition to its light can be detected? For even the single portion that the moon adds each day is noticeable, just as its decrease is also perceptible. And is the sun itself, then, a vessel that is not full? And how is its lack not visible? And if it has lost nothing, how does it receive anything? For if it were complete and its interior full of its light— as indeed it is full—a full vessel cannot receive anything more if you pour it into it. For whatever falls into it overflows.
