But this full vessel, which receives none of what the Manichaeans speak of, cries out to us by its very appearance that we should accept nothing from the Manichaeans. But let us leave aside these things that the Manichaeans say, since they alone bear witness to them. And let us listen to the things Moses says, to which all the nations under heaven bear witness. First are the Hebrews, who reckon by the moon, and after them all the nations, those called barbarians, and also the Greeks, who use the solar reckoning, although they do not abandon the lunar reckoning either. And now, even if we are making our discussion lengthy, let us show what is counted by the solar reckoning and what is counted by the lunar reckoning. By the solar reckoning are counted the days. For the coming of light and darkness is known from the sun. This is what distinguishes a day. But months are known from the moon, for the beginning and end of months are determined by the moon. For the sun, whose rising and setting distinguish the days, does not distinguish the months, because its course proceeds uniformly. It shows no distinctive change when thirty days have passed, so that one could know from that change whether a month has ended or begun. It is the moon that distinguishes the months by waxing and waning. It does not distinguish the days. For how often does it happen that it rises at the third or fourth hour and sets at the seventh or ninth, while for two whole days it is not visible at all! God, in his anger, who also arranged the months for reckoning and the days for counting, made the sun for counting the days, just as he also made the moon for counting the months. And just as they complete a day through its course, In the same way, the moon too completes its months: from its beginning to its end it brings forth thirty days. Now if a day consists of twelve hours, and the sun travels a course of twelve hours, it is clear that the sun is the source of the days. And again, if a month consists of thirty days, and the moon, as it wanes and becomes full, completes thirty days, it is clear that the moon too is the mother and source of the months. The exact reckoning, however, is twenty-nine and a half. This too is the Creator's wisdom, which combined and arranged the numbers at the beginning to complete the reckoning. For when the days are counted numerically, a month consists of thirty days. But as for these eleven days that [?] after [?] did not arrange—and why, and for what purpose, does the moon fall short by eleven days at a time? And why are three hours each year left over in the sun's course? These three are an exalted mystery [?], as the numbering indicates and the calculation explains: because of the deficiency that exists in the moon, months are intercalated, and because of the surplus that exists in the sun, days are intercalated, so that through the intercalation of months and days this luminary may be humbled, and God's lordship may be known. Because many peoples have gone astray through them on account of their light, he exposed the fault in their reckoning, showing that they should not be worshiped because of their neediness. For if the sun's reckoning is not put in order, the moon's course, through its swiftness and its deficiency, changes the seasons of the year for them, so that summer turns into winter and winter into summer. And again, if there were no deficiency in the moon, requiring it to be made complete by the sun, these three extra hours belonging to the sun would have no place to go and remain in the numbering and reckoning of the year. For among the complete days, the three hundred and sixty-five days, where could the three extra hours enter and stand? They cannot be counted with the full number of the months, nor do they stand within the complete number of the days. But between the moon's months and the reckoning of the sun's days, the Lord of the luminaries prepared a place for them to go and remain. We have spoken of these things in passing, since we had not been called to speak about them. But we were compelled to speak in order to rebuke those who wished to divert the luminaries from their service of marking months and days, so as to demonstrate in them shadows rising from the earth. And because the moon is made for a reckoning of thirty days and consists entirely of these portions, once the thirty days have ended, it no longer exists. For it is not itself one thing and its light another. And since that moon is, they say, a vessel into which the luminary is poured, even if that light diminished as light, the vessel's own substance, along with that of the light, could not by its nature come to an end or increase. All vessels bear witness that their own substance remains within the measure of their nature: they do not grow larger if more is put into them, nor do they disappear if less is put into them. And if whatever is in them is emptied out and comes to an end, the vessels themselves do not come to an end. And because they call the moon a ship of light, let an illustration drawn from a ship serve to refute them: whether it is filled or emptied, it remains within the measure of its own substance, that is, its length and width together with its height. But this ship of light which they say exists in heaven— The light poured into it or emptied out of it is visible to us, but the ship itself is not visible. Or let them show us the vessel itself, so that we may know that it is designed for this purpose: to become full and be emptied, as they say. Or whether the vessel itself is what becomes full and is built up, rises, becomes complete, is hidden, and descends. This is apparent even to the blind who cannot see: the moon was made for counting the months, not for purification. And if they say that it is not visible because it is very transparent and fine, how, then, is the sun visible? For its light is clearer and purer than the moon's. And is it because of its transparency that it goes and comes every day to the house of life, as they say? And which account should we listen to—that of Bardaisan, who said of the moon that it is an earth and a womb, filled from the lofty, upper abundance and pouring out upon the lowly and those below? Or that of Mani, who said that it is filled from below and sends to the upper regions? But both of them lied in both their accounts, so that the statement of Moses might stand firm, who said of the luminaries, “Let them be for signs and for seasons,” and the rest. But who would not laugh at these childish statements: that the luminaries ultimately became [?] for Mani's followers? If only they were for something important! But they are for belches. For it is through these that the light is purified—if it is purified at all. There is no evidence that it is purified through prayer, as they say. But that it is purified through belching—its taste bears witness to this. If not, let them pray and belch, and let experience convince them without argument which of the two has the taste of food: prayer or belching. There is further evidence: the person belching looks upward, as though, with the force and rush of air, he would send upward what is being purified, to the place from which it had descended. Perhaps this mystery exists secretly in the world, and the world was not aware of it. Perhaps even Mani himself was not aware of it. Here it is not the person who prays a great deal who is purified, but the person who belches a great deal. For physicians too, using various substances, stimulate many belches to [?] the stomach that has not digested. For whenever someone does not belch, evidence appears of the stomach's heaviness and coldness. Unless it digests, it does not release; unless it releases, he does not belch; if he does not belch, it does not come out; and if it does not come out, it is not purified. For coldness holds the food fast there—that is, the cold phlegm that lies above the food. It is a great enemy of Mani's followers, for in its coldness it seeks to pile itself upon it— upon that which is to be purified—so that it will not be released and come out of there. And so an enemy to their enemy can be a pungent [?], which enters and fights, grappling with it as in a contest and tearing apart the covering that is spread over the food. Then a path is opened for the imprisoned light there, so that its purified portion may come out in a belch. And what about when the Manichaeans vomit? For since their food had not yet been digested, he knew that their purification had not yet ascended either. And one must say that their light is still mixed into their vomit. They ought to swallow it down again, so that the light hidden in it does not remain in a state of corruption. Especially if a dog comes and swallows it: then that light which came out in vomit from inside the Manichaean who is called righteous has entered and been imprisoned in the stomach of a filthy dog. That is, instead of the imprisoned light quickly gaining an ascent on high if that Manichaean had swallowed his vomit again, so that it could fly up to its Father's house, that Manichaean ought to be tormented on its account, because he knows that the light has entered and been imprisoned in a dog's belly. From there it was cast out in an emission into the dog's offspring, and that light was transmitted through a race of savage creatures and biters. It must necessarily be savage like them and bite like them. And it ought to bite and tear apart the Manichaean who vomited it up and did not swallow it again, because he was the cause of this savagery for it. And if they say that it is purified even in a dog, then dogs surpass them in purification, and ought to be fed more than they are. And if they say that the air purifies it and carries it upward, they have unwillingly admitted that it is purified not by prayer but by other agencies, whether those that dry, those that cook, those that heat, or those that cool. For if, as they say, the pleasant flavor found in foods belongs to the luminous being mixed into them, then, just as the mouth perceived that sweetness of the light when it entered, it ought to perceive it again when it comes out. For if it perceived it when it entered while mixed with bitterness, how much more ought the mouth to perceive it when it comes out, once its sweetness has been separated and is entirely on its own! But if it perceived it when it entered, yet does not perceive it when it comes out in purification, it has become clear that this sweetness belongs not to the nature that was purified, but to its opposite. For something that can be felt and tasted when it enters must necessarily be felt and tasted when it comes out as well. But if they go on lying, they go on exposing themselves. For if they say that the mouth does not perceive the light because it has become subtle and purified, this little statement undoes their entire construction: how, then, did the primordial Darkness even seize the primordial luminous being, touch it, feel it, eat it, savor it, taste it, and swallow it? For look: this mouth shares the nature of that Darkness, yet it does not even perceive it at all when it comes out from within it. Here their entire deceit has been exposed. Because a sound ear has encountered it. For this purified substance that comes out of the mouth has not been completely purified. That is why it goes from the mouth to the moon, and from the moon to the sun, to be purified and become as it was before. For if it is purified and does not need the moon’s purification, why must it go to the moon, and from the moon to the sun, rather than fly straight away, ascend, and rise to its own place? It sits idle here for fifteen days until the moon is emptied, and then it empties out after thirty days. Or is it perhaps because it has forgotten the way to its own people’s home? And how does it know how to go, since it does not know its way, and another sends it? And it must again be fed [?]. It cannot even go to the moon and it is another who must eat [?] they should place it in the moon. But if both are one nature, how does one lead while the other is led, and one knows how to feed what shares its nature, while the other does not know? And how do the children of the one who knows everything not know how to go to their home, from which they came? And who could be patient with these people except the Truth, who desires their repentance, who wholly rebukes these things so that they themselves may not go astray in this way? If, then, this substance that comes out of the mouth, although it has the taste of filth and mixture in it, is so clear and fine when it leaves the mouth that the mouth does not perceive it as it is purified—and it is purified and clearer than it was before the mingling and mixture—how can turbid darkness touch that clear substance which cannot be felt? Or how can something bodily seize that spiritual substance which cannot be touched, or something corporeal eat something incorporeal? Either darkness is clear, purified, and fine, and light is corporeal by nature, or both are fine, or [?] neither perceives the other. Just as they were perceived during chewing, they should be perceived during purification. And if both are light, where does this heaviness come from? And if they are clear, the turbidity entered from somewhere else. And consequently we must seek that other entity which disturbed both of them. Even if it is found, these same things that were said about them [?] are still said about it [?] why not [?] go [?] without compulsion. But if that light were God, whether he were good or just, his goodness and justice would have required him to surround his realm with a strong wall and preserve his freedom and dignity from his contemptible enemy and his shameless neighbor, especially since the Good One would have perceived that his nature was vulnerable to harm, as they say. Far be it that this should be said of a good one who betrays! But if, out of shame, they turn around and say that he cannot even be harmed, then whom are they teaching? Is it not the one who has gone astray? And whom are they healing? Is it not the one who has been wounded? And whom are they teaching confession? Is it not the one who has denied and blasphemed? For these evils, together with countless others, have happened and continue to happen to the souls that come from him. And even if they did not come from him but were nevertheless in his realm, he would have been obliged, as one who is wise and loves his possessions, to surround his vulnerable portions with a protective wall. This creation, which was fashioned by a wise Creator, offers convincing evidence concerning these things. For because he knew that human beings act recklessly in their freedom, and venture by their own will to set limits to creation. Because they cannot set a limit to creation—for its binding constraints did not allow them—they ventured to set a limit to it through inquiry. Just as they also wanted to build a tower [?], so that by it they might ascend to where no one can ascend. For the ladder to that height is the grace of its Creator. Even in thousands and tens of thousands of years, they could not have ascended to that height to which Elijah ascended in the blink of an eye. For it is not a tower that brings someone up to heaven, because it is the will of the Lord of heaven that brings someone up to heaven. So that kings might not act presumptuously, now as then, he placed them within creation, which cannot be conquered. For if they would ascend above, there are outstretched heights that cannot be measured. If they would descend below, there are dreadful depths that cannot be explored. If they would cross to the ends, there are bitter seas that have no bounds. And these things [?] he who cannot be harmed was afraid for himself, but rather it was for it —our freedom—that he had compassion, so that our presumption would not be crushed by something that does it no good. And if creation is so fortified against human beings, weak as they are, the realm of the Good One, who is supposedly superior in his very being, ought all the more to have been fortified against dreadful enemies. For just as the lord of the realm is perfect in his being, so his realm too ought to be well ordered and its structure fortified. And that structure ought also to have been fortified with a wall of will. But the realm lacks a wall, and its lord lacks forethought. And if he did not fortify it with a [?] wall, he himself was deficient in this. How can they call someone God who is far inferior even to human beings? For there is no one who has not made a door and a bolt for his house. Or perhaps they argue against these things too: that there should be no walls for a city, no fortification for a refuge, and no stronghold for deliverance, no fence for a vineyard, and no enclosure for a flock. And who, indeed, among their number has not shut his door or the door of his congregation? But the doors that are shut here were fortified because of the danger. They [?] for themselves [?] was [?] being released from these things. Because that danger is great. And if a band of raiders had come against Mani in the East and against his disciples, would they not have taken refuge in a fortress, sought shelter in a stronghold, and gone inside a wall? But I suppose they are wiser than their father, whom they say is God. For they know how to do these things, even though they are clothed in a thoroughly confusing body. But their father, who is not clothed in an intoxicating body, does not know how to do these things in his realm. And if Mani’s followers do not flee before a band of raiders and do not take refuge in a fortress or behind a wall, let us ask whether it is because their bodies cannot be harmed. And if they look forward to this very thing—to being killed and breaking free of the body—and have no need of a wall, up above, in their father’s house, they had all the greater need of walls, so that they would not become mingled with the hateful body. For because of the absence of walls, which they did not have, darkness swallowed them and mingled them with this body. And while they look forward to breaking free of it by means of the sword, But even this is not true. Yet they escaped from it by means of walls. And suppose someone tells me that there were no stones. Or was there a great expanse of earth from which the master builder cut a solid stone for the tomb of Darkness? Where is there blindness like this—with such a stonecutter and such cut stones? And where did all this work take place? And where is this skilled apprentice, the architect of its tomb, who stretched out a measuring line, weighed a plumb bob, straightened the [?], and knew [?]? Was there really no one to give it advice, so that they might take possession of their territory and guard it? And look, they have escaped the ten thousand evils that surround them today. But if they again reject these arguments, they are arguing against everything that is right, so that only things that are not right may be proclaimed. And if they are so boastful while they are mistaken, as though they had found something true—for error has deceived these erring people who have found error. Yet it was they themselves who, through their own free choice, were found by it according to its will. But because of these boastful people who hold their heads high, let us withdraw a little from our argument and leave them alone on one point, so that they may be duly convicted on another. For Darkness was never pleased to leave its place, because every entity that exists, if it does exist, rests in its own place, since it is the place suited to its nature: like fish in water, like moles in the soil, like a moth in clothing, like a woodworm in wood, like a weevil in a storehouse, like a swallow in an inhabited place, and like an owl in a ruin, like a dove in the light and like a bat at night. For these, along with many others, are pleased with the dwelling place suited to their nature. And if someone exchanges what belongs to them for what does not belong to them— that is, places suited to them for places not suited to them, for places not suited to them—it is a great evil and a bitter disaster for them. This is how the glorious psalm of blessed David recounts them, listing and showing the places of them all, in Psalm 104, which begins, “Bless the Lord, my soul. Lord my God, you are very great.” It shows that their places correspond to their natures, and their rest likewise corresponds to their places. For if you bathe a fish in oil, bury a mole in honey, lodge a moth in silver and a woodworm in gold, and a weevil in a heap of pearls, although these things are far more precious than what belongs to them, they rest in what belongs to them. And if these things, which are made and are not self-existent, rest in the places created for them, how much more does the self-existent entity of Darkness rest in the abode suited to its nature! And if anyone prods it to leave that abode, it suffers. It is like the mole of darkness whenever someone brings it up out of its place, the darkness. For if Darkness had a place of its own, as they say—something that is difficult to believe— But the difficulty for it is that Darkness, they say, exchanged its natural place, loved what was contrary to its nature, and exchanged its customary way for something foreign to its nature. For even an infant moves from its place to another place, both of which belong to it; and although it has come from what is its own to what is its own, it certainly cries when it comes out. How much more would the Being be killed if someone uprooted it from its place to another place that did not belong to it! For just as it enjoys peace in its own place, so in a place not its own it experiences a chill. Physicians too say that anything that does not preserve nature destroys the [?] of nature, although they are speaking about habit, not nature. For if someone sets out to become accustomed to something to which he is not accustomed, unless he wisely changes his habit little by little, he is harmed by it. Now if something to which a person is not accustomed injures that person when he encounters it suddenly, even though it belongs to his nature, although not to his accustomed way, how did Darkness suddenly encounter Light, its opposite, [?] its heir? And instead of inevitably being harmed, as nature testifies it should have been, it actually rushed upon it, as the falsehood babbled about Light says, when that true [?]. It says what is true, for when people lie, they suffer distress. If that accompanied it, it would truly suffer distress. But when that counterfeit was crushed by truth's questions, its entire construction was revealed and exposed. Just as Moses' pestle crushed the cast-metal calf, so the power of truth crushed the fabricated teaching. I know, however, that although the calf was crushed, the Jews did not abandon the worship of the calf. Likewise, although the teaching of Mani's followers has been exposed, the Manichaeans do not denounce the worship of the sun and moon. For they resemble one another in their blasphemies, even though they do not resemble one another in their scriptures. For just as the Jews blasphemed against the New Testament, those people blasphemed against our Old Testament. He, however, is the new wine and the old. He is old because his flavor remains in him and his fragrance has not faded; he is new because the ferment of his power and his mighty love stirs within him. As for the vessels, those who did not receive the old wine condemned themselves by their filth, and they were not worthy to contain it. And those who did not receive the new wine are worn-out wineskins, which he exposed by his strength as unable to [?].
The second discourse is finished.

The third discourse against the teaching. I wish to offer yet another reply against all three of them—that is, first against Marcion: even if heaven were found beneath the Stranger, let us ask who supports the heavens and everything in them. For power is needed to support them. Or perhaps the Stranger's heavens rest upon the Maker's heavens, so that the Maker is the upholder of everything—as indeed he is.

But if they say that the Stranger's heavens hang by the power of the Fiery One, we too deal crookedly with the crooked: he who is above the heavens cannot support the heavens unless he is below them. But if he himself is above the heavens and he himself is below them, It is known that this is the place of his possessions, and within it are held those souls that Jesus brought up from here. For a bearer is needed for these heavy souls that he brought up from here. That is very plausible! His possessions were found to be within his bosom [?]. He and his burdens need another power to carry them. For we cannot accept this from them, just as they themselves did not accept it from us: that something should be set in place without a foundation. And as for the body, although they come from darkness, as they say, they have speech; and for [?] adornment, and there is no [?], and for touch [?], and for swift light, which comes from a speaking nature that has shut their mouths, like a scorpion [?] it has. Let them be rebuked concerning light, because they are lamps for our service, created. Rightly are the sun and moon deprived of speech, because through speech [?] and our service, God, humanity [?] against them [?] are found. For, even unwillingly, they confirm the statement that Moses wrote. For when God created everything for the service of humanity, to make known that the creatures were created for its service, he did not give them speech and thought as he did to humanity. Their lowliness bears witness that they serve, just as humanity’s exalted position bears witness that it is served. He had not created only tame creatures for Adam’s service. For it might have been thought that, if there were tame creatures, they could humble him. For this reason God created those that are fierce, those that are terrifying, those that are bitter, and those that are tame, so that Adam’s lordship might be seen resting over them all, like God’s. He had this authority over them before he sinned. But they took this authority over him after he sinned. So God said, “Let us make a human being in our image,” that is, in the image of his authority. For just as God’s authority reigns over everything, so the yoke of Adam’s lordship was laid upon everything. So let those who speak against the God of Moses tell us how they can speak against Scripture, when they themselves are witnesses to its truth. For Scripture showed that it was to humanity that God gave his greatness and authority over the earth and everything in it. And look, [?] this [?] that it is so. But according to the erring people’s own book, they do not give honor and greatness to humanity alone, but to all the portions of light, because they come, they say, from one great and honored nature. And because they wanted to give worship to these things that serve, those Manichaeans, worshipers of the sun, compelled humanity, which is served, to offer worship to creation. But see how they are rebuked by the creatures themselves. For it is evident that they have exalted the sun and moon above humanity. Let them tell us which is greater: something great in its light and radiance, or something great in its speech and knowledge? If what is great in light is superior, let them erase their books, abolish their teachings, silence their words, renounce their faith, and sit down and weep over themselves. And why do they not have radiance like fire? If radiance is what is great [?] they are also called to account: if they come from it, from the nature that shines, why do they not have the radiance of that which shares their nature? Suppose someone were to kindle a fire in the wilderness by striking flint or something else, making a great blaze there from a large heap: between that fire, great as it is and possessing great radiance, and a small human being possessing an excellent mind, which is greater? For if the fire’s rays, which travel over many mountains, [?] can be contained, the rays of the hidden mind cannot be contained within this creation: it is not large enough to hold them. For a lamp contained inside a vessel can demonstrate that every light that exists can be contained within some enclosure. But there is no enclosure that can contain the mind. For it is contained in the body, yet is greater than it; within creation, yet exceeds it; within the embrace of creation, yet creation is not large enough for it. It is without limit, because its reach extends even to God, who cannot be bounded. Then let them either be properly persuaded or be severely scourged by questioning. Or is the human being more honored than everything, with all creatures given to serve him? Or, if the nature of light is a single principle, as they say, why are the portions of this light that are in a deaf person deaf, and those in a blind person opposed to us, and those in a mute person silent, and those in a scorpion bitter and stinging? And if evil has overpowered and defeated them, look: in doves and lambs the good portions are numerous. Why, then, are those in doves not shrewd, and those in lambs not wise? And so shrewdness and wisdom have been found to belong to darkness [?], because this darkness is shrewd by its own stock [?], and the ignorance of that good nature [?]. Simplicity, however, and ignorance, which exist [?] from [?]. Likewise, at all times the simplicity of that good nature has been and continues to be defeated by the cunning of the evil nature. For the one also has strength, and the other also has wisdom. For the lion, the wolf, and the dragon testify that they are shrewd and deceitful, wise and strong, just as the lamb and the dove testify that they are weak and ignorant. Thus ignorance and weakness are attached to that nature whose portions are numerous in them. But if they bring another comparison, saying, “Look, darkness testifies to its own weakness, since it is always defeated by the light,” they have unwittingly exposed and laid bare the foundations of their teaching. For there they recount how darkness defeated the [?] and swallowed him. But perhaps they boast of this: “Look, we enchant the serpent and charm the scorpion.” They say that the serpent’s cunning is defeated by the charm, and along with it the scorpion’s gall is also enchanted and overcome. The test has shown these men to be wise, since their wisdom has overcome even the serpent’s cunning! Yet their wisdom has been made a laughingstock by the demon’s cunning. For the demon submits in order to bring others into submission, and lets himself be cast as their servant in order to become their master. For he accommodates himself to them in things that do him no harm, so that they may yield to him in things through which they die. For the demon, because of his subtle nature, enters the serpent, just as he hid in it from the beginning. And just as Adam and his household supposed that it was the serpent speaking with them, and because they were unwilling to attend to the hidden being dwelling in it, they were drawn after the outward voice calling them, so, while they thought they had been persuaded by the serpent, they had become disciples of Satan within it, without realizing it. But let us pass over this briefly, because this is not the time to finish the serpent’s whole story. Yet even though we are leaving his story, we are coming back to the story of his disciples. It is as though we were going from the serpent to the serpent’s children. Thus, although it is the demon who does everything through the serpent, at the time of the incantation the demon does not reveal himself or show that he is there. For he knows that they would flee from him because he is hateful. Instead, he makes it appear that it is the serpent that submits to the incantation, so that they will believe that this incantation too comes from God, and so that, when they are persuaded to learn the incantation because of the serpent, they will be persuaded to serve Satan through the incantation. Let us therefore ask the serpent’s children about the serpent: how is it persuaded, or how is it subjected by an incantation belonging to something of another nature, when the children of the Evil One, as they say, are not persuaded by an incantation? How, then, can it be a single nature, part of which is overcome and part of which is not? If it is the incantation that is powerful, why has it not subjected all the parts of the Evil One? And if the Evil One is more powerful than the incantation, [?] the one who was persuaded. And if the power of the Good One is mingled in this incantation, and the name of the True One is associated with it, so that it becomes a weapon by which serpents and scorpions and all the enemy’s power are overcome, was there really not a single lightning bolt or enchanter in the Good One’s realm who could have gone out and enchanted that great dragon which attacked them from the beginning? But perhaps the sons of light had not yet learned this incantation. And from whom, then, did this discovery come later? Perhaps because this incantation had not yet been learned, that torrent which slipped out of its place and swallowed the innocent sons of light was not bound. And what authority did Jesus give his disciples to overcome serpents and scorpions: the authority of an incantation, or the authority of faith? And if faith comes from God, acknowledge that incantation comes from Satan. Therefore it is he who, in his cunning, has prepared such bonds for himself, allowing himself to be bound so that he can bind others: when they come to bind him with an incantation, he in turn binds them with paganism. And how do they speak of the primeval human beings? For they have also gone far astray over this name. They lead them to understand the Scriptures backwards. For this statement is written in the Gospel: “That life is the light of man.” But the Greek Gospel explains that that life is the light of human beings. They constructed their interpretation from the word “man,” as it is written in Aramaic, making this “man” into the Primal Man, the father of the luminous [?] whom they call the Splendors. Those whom Bardaisan made into five beings, Mani made from a single being. This battle is not ours. We ought to remove ourselves from between the two serpents, so that they can fight each other for a victory that is entirely a defeat. On the other hand, because Mani could not find another way out for himself, he unwillingly entered through the door that Bardaisan had opened. For when they saw this body, so beautifully put together, its seven senses arranged in order, the heart, which is the instrument of the soul’s movements, and the tongue, which is the lyre of speech, they were ashamed to blaspheme against it openly. So they resorted to cunning and divided it between two sides. They attributed its nature to the Evil One and its making to the archon, and the cause of its formation to Wisdom. She, they say, showed the image of its beauty to the archon and the governor. Through it she deceived them, so that, eager to make something like what they had seen, each of them would give from his treasury something of what he possessed. By this means their treasuries would be emptied of what they had seized. And when Mani saw at this point that he could not cross the river anywhere else, he was forced to come and cross where Bardaisan had crossed. For he too said this about the Primal Man: that through the image he showed the sons of darkness, he compelled them. And because both of them say the same thing here, the same thing is said against both, so that through the truth, which is not divided against itself, these two divided men may be defeated. For in this statement they have joined together against the truth. But a single statement spoken by the true apostle dismantles their constructions without effort. For he said, “Your bodies are temples of God, and whoever destroys God’s temple, God will destroy.” If, then, the body belongs to corruption, as those who have abandoned hope for their bodies say, why is the person who destroys it himself destroyed? After all, even if no one destroys it, it is a body belonging to corruption. But if whoever destroys it is himself destroyed, it is clear that its architect and maker is God, and not the sons of darkness, as Mani said, nor the foolish governor, as Bardaisan said.
The fourth discourse is finished.
The fifth discourse, against the false teaching.

Faithful listening is the likeness of a chaste betrothed woman, who is not drawn after unfamiliar voices. An ear that strays even a little from the truth resembles an adulteress who strays from her partner. And an ear that is led along by every teaching resembles a prostitute, who to everyone [?] she resembles, who to everyone who calls her consents. Rebuke, then, the distracted listening that was corrupted by the liar’s voices, because instead of the name of the true bridegroom, it loved the name of its corrupter. For he consented in his mind that Mani’s name should be pronounced over it, and not Christ’s name. And because this is the teaching that came from the school of Marcion, Valentinus, and Bardaisan, and he is the last of them all—this is the bottom sediment: as it is fouler than what is above it, so this is fouler than those who preceded him. In the world’s evil time this teaching sprang up, at the end of the world, and because it fought fiercely against the truth. Let us say a little against him—or rather, not we, but the truth itself speaks against him. Now the subject of this teaching, though it appears small and contemptible, resembles—to simple people, those who do not believe in it—the hole in the wall that blessed Ezekiel saw. Although the hole itself was contemptible and small, great evils, much filth, and hidden, shameful things were inside it. Now that word which commanded Ezekiel to dig through the wall, which was a covering over the abomination— by the power of that holy word, let us too break through the covering of the impure teaching, so that the abominations inside it may be exposed. But I do not wish to recount them all, because they are foul. Likewise, even the holy prophet could not make his mouth a passage for the filth that is foul and deadly. [?] But let us imitate the illustrious prophet: just as he said as much as it was possible to say, so he too said what he said, though not everything, but only some things, since the discerning can understand what is left out from what is said. The holy voice therefore commanded the prophet, who was obedient in everything: “Go in and see the great abominations they commit here.” He went in and saw all the [?] of the house of Israel, depicted on the wall. Likewise Mani also painted on a scroll with colors, as some of his disciples say, those images of paganism that he invented in his mind. He gave the ugly figures the name “sons of darkness,” so that [?] to his disciples the ugliness of darkness, so that they would recoil from it. And he gave the beautiful figures the name “sons of light,” supposedly to show them its beauty as well, so that they would long for it. As he said: “I wrote them in books and painted them in colors, so that whoever hears them spoken may also see them in an image, and whoever cannot learn them from [?] may learn them from a picture.” Perhaps he even worshiped those deadly things depicted there. The voice spoke again to the prophet: “Turn again, and you will see abominations greater than these.” He went in and saw women sitting and weeping for Tammuz. In what way, then, was this abomination greater than those before it? It was because those pagan images were thought to be images of the living God, but here the worthless and adulterous Tammuz was both worshiped and mourned. For this reason it was greater than the others. And now, corresponding to those idle mourning women who wept for the god Tammuz, who was killed by a wild boar because of his adultery—a boar that they too regard as a god— come and see here also the idle women of Mani’s community, those whom they call “righteous women.” Because he far surpassed them in wickedness, they too sit idle over the radiant ones, the sons of the luminaries, whom darkness, they say, came out and swallowed. Again the one giving the command said to the one receiving it: “Turn again, and you will see abominations greater than these.” He went in and saw, between the platform and the altar—for the altar for their offerings had been built on a platform— about twenty-five men, with their backs toward the temple of the Lord. By the term “their backs,” he referred indirectly to their private parts, for it was this shameful nakedness that they displayed toward the temple of the Holy One. This sin was greater than the earlier ones and those in between. These, it is said, are the ones. They used to rise early and worship the sun. And it is written about them that they worshiped the sun alone. But Mani added to this and taught his disciples to worship the moon as well. For they worship the sun and the moon—lights through which their worshipers became dark. When the sun comes to the west, they too worship toward the west, like their relatives the Marcionites. For it was not through this act of worship that their inward kinship would be joined together. And because his name [?] who said, “Not [?] God [?] to say to [?].” That is, what comes from [?] and happened [?] turned [?] and an occurrence such that, at the neck, [?] this [?] they are, those from whom he turned toward [?] him [?] set a limit for him who is limited. They want to flee from him. They worship [?] while [?], because even [?] is full, and from his greatness. For if the sky is enclosed at the opening through which someone wishes to pass, it is found behind him at another opening in front of him. How much more, then, is he everywhere, whom openings and places cannot contain! But those abominations that Ezekiel saw were perhaps a symbol of these [?] of Mani’s followers. They begin in this way: for at the beginning he posited two self-existent beings and two regions, and two natures and two roots. Let us therefore inquire about the two, whether there are only two. For each one of these two, because it is one, must necessarily be like itself throughout. But if there is something in it unlike itself, it is falsely called one. For it is clear that whatever is unlike it in nature does not belong to its nature. Let us now hear him as he describes [?] one among many that do not resemble it in nature, nor does it resemble them, nor do they resemble one another. First he posits space. And how does space resemble God? One sets limits, while the other is not limited; one contains, while the other is not contained. One has individual existence, knowledge, power, and wisdom, and in him are goodness and freedom, while the other has not even one of these. Yet there is a great inquiry concerning space that cannot be denied. For space is unlike not only God, but also [?] itself, dark and light, as they say there are there. And let the inquiry be strangled by the question—that is, it is a noose that they themselves have placed around their necks. For let them be questioned about space itself: whether half of it is dark and half light, and whether half of it is good and half evil, and whether its sides facing the Good resemble the Good, and its openings facing the Good resemble the Good, and its openings facing the Bitter One resemble darkness. If they say that the half facing the Good is good, and the half facing the Evil One is evil, this is difficult to accept: since the space containing both of them is one, how can half of it be good and half evil? For they cannot do away with the two regions. And if they posit another space between one region and the other, a third question arises about this third space as well: what is it, whose is it, and whom does it resemble? Necessarily, the space that contains them is one. Many divisions and boundaries are also found within it. For boundaries do not define and limit space, as he imagined it; rather, they define the things within space—that is, houses or cities, or lands, or mountains and plains, or kingdoms and nations that border one another at the sea. And on dry land. But if they say that space is uniform throughout, extending over both the Good One and the Evil One, it is clear that either it belongs to both of them, or both of them belong to it. For under one yoke, which has fallen upon both self-existent beings, both have become subject to the great yoke that has come to rule over them. And hence they are also divided. For the equal yoke laid upon them has not allowed them to refuse to submit to its equality themselves. Besides this, an entity within space cannot fill that entire space. Otherwise, picture in your mind that whatever is within space and has a body must itself be bounded. For the space that bounds it is greater than it. But something that is not within space is not bounded. There is no space to bound it. Therefore, the greatness that they attribute to space in their teaching is attributed to God himself by the teaching of truth. For he is his own space. Indeed, the praises that Bardaisan uttered concerning space are great, greater than those he uttered concerning God, who is within space—praises that are appropriate not to space, but to God himself. For if they are appropriate to space itself, their space turns out to be superior to their God. But the word claims these praises, the true word, treating them as acts of worship and offering them to the one who is great and worthy of worship. For just as it is not right to worship an idol, so that there should not be many gods alongside the One, so it is not right to call space a self-existent being alongside God. And just as it is not right to posit another power capable of commanding God, so it is not right to posit a space capable of bounding God. For if he is subjected in either respect, that is a great blasphemy. For just as he is not the commander of all if he is commanded, so he is not the one who bounds all if he is bounded. For if a ruler is answerable to his lordship, space too is answerable to his lordship. For if all rulers are under his authority, as they themselves say, all spaces are also contained within his greatness, as we ourselves say—that is, as truth requires. He went on to say that this God also has a luminous earth and dwells upon it. Just as he made him dependent on space, so he made him dependent on earth. For he did not say that the earth was made and prepared for his possessions, as the prophet of truth said concerning the God of truth: “He did not create it in vain, but so that his creation might dwell in it.” And just as he made the earth for those below, he also made heaven for those above. Both were for the sake of beings made and created, spiritual and bodily. For before his creatures existed, he did not need heaven in order to dwell upon it, just as he did not need space in order to exist within it. As for Mani and Marcion, one the first and the other the last, with Bardaisan in the middle, a single question extends to all three. But let Marcion be questioned first, since he was the earliest: if those heavens belong to the Stranger as something self-existent, it is clear that there is not just one self-existent being. But two that do not resemble each other, even if space encompasses him. Here again are three self-existent beings: space does not resemble heaven, nor do either of them resemble God. God turns out to be weaker and smaller than both of them. For space is found to encompass him as something small, and heaven to carry him as someone weak—apart from other things, which we will not discuss at length. These very same arguments also turn against Mani. For he names space and earth together with God as self-existent. But Bardaisan, taking a crafty middle course, chose one and rejected the other. He did this to rebuke his neighbor with it. He does not know that what he was ashamed of is the counterpart of what he admitted. For he said that God is within space, but did not call it self-existent. He did not place him in heaven like Marcion, nor on earth like Mani. But he was ashamed [?] these things, so that there would not be found [?] carrying God. He does not know that there is something outside God that encompasses him. And there is something beneath God that carries him [?] something [?] carries them [?] he attached it to him [?] a space of his own, like God. If, however, one of them is above, both present difficulties; and if one is easy to explain, both are, as stated above. For both also stand or fall together, so that either that one is refuted like this one, or this one is established like that one. But Mani adds still more and makes them numerous: five natures, as the impostor called them. And how is this possible, if he posits two roots within each of which many are contained? For how can there be from it [?] light that is from it, while from it [?]? And from it, while [?] one [?] without [?] wind to fire; they demonstrate their nature, just as water and light also demonstrate that their root is not one. For the author of this teaching was foolish, even though he was crafty. He spoke of two roots so that we would not say to him, as Bardaisan said, "Five roots." They have no reason for dividing one nature into many natures, those that are combined [?] that one; they are not one another [?]. And this is a refutation of both of them. If he dared [?] there is there [?] from both of them to both of them, if a body, many [?] burning for them [?] how water [?] it [?] even without attaching it, it is darkness that he sets up as the opponent of the self-existent beings. Those self-existent beings are found to harm one another, if they are self-existent. For this is what their self-existence requires, and experience also demonstrates it. But if they are created from nothing, the Maker can, if he wishes, make them peaceful toward one another, or make them hostile toward one another, so that they harm and are harmed. From now on, let us ask briefly about these two roots, leaving aside the many complications of their statements: whether they were attached to one another, or whether they were far apart, or whether one was below and one above. And if he says that they existed opposite one another, Marcion and Bardaisan are subtler than he is. For Bardaisan posits darkness as the lower one, below everything. And Marcion maintains that the Stranger is above everything. But if the place in which they all dwell is one, and that place cannot be measured in length or bounded in width, why were all those self-existent beings found dwelling in a single neighborhood, one above another or one behind another? Could they not have happened to be scattered and separated from one another in that boundless place? This very thing demonstrates that their teaching is an embellished human invention. For the reason for this proximity of their gods, who are close to one another, shows that, because the people who are in error are close to one another, they therefore brought their gods close [?] to one another. And because they themselves are enclosed within a single region of creation, for that very reason he confined their gods within one place. And because they cannot go outside this world, lest the argument be raised against them, “Where did you become aware of these gods?” they devised a scheme and fabricated reasons for summoning their gods into this world, so that it would appear that they had received from them the revealed teaching about their hidden mysteries. And like children playing on broad steps, when one sits on the lowest step, as though to provoke him, his companion sits on the middle step; and as though to challenge them both, another sits on the highest step. This is how the preachers of error behaved. To challenge one another, they named places that outdo one another and gods who are higher than their companions. Their story amounts to children's play. For among children there are some who are bigger than others, and there are also steps that are higher than others. They, however, named empty places and useless gods that do not exist, and foolish tales that have no foundation. And because Mani saw that his two brothers who were older than he—that is, Marcion and Bardaisan—had preceded him, one naming the lower region and the other the upper region, he saw that if he said “below,” it had already been said, and if he said “above,” he had already been anticipated. Not knowing how to position those two self-existent beings that he introduced, when he saw that above and below were occupied, he placed them opposite one another on an equal level. For he too prophesied by the same spirit as his brothers. And it has been said that the teaching about matter is found among them all. For only in the Church is it not found. And if matter is an evil self-existent being, as they testify, because the Church does not proclaim it, [?] in the Church. It is not present in the Church, because it is not in the Church's Scripture. Among them all it is present in its entirety, because it is found in its entirety in their books. And if Mani and Bardaisan named gods who were makers, perhaps this gave them a way to name matter as well. For it is precisely the cause of creative activity, as they say. Who compelled Marcion to recount it, tear his tunic, and dance with the empty-headed in our works [?]? For if he said that the Stranger was not a maker, this would have been enough for his error: to say that the Good One, who had not made anything, came and gave life to the Maker's children. And because his dispute was with the Creator, he had no need to introduce the account of matter. And if it was to show that the Maker deceived matter, that Stranger likewise did not keep faith with it, since he came and wore them down with fasting and prayer— the body that comes from matter. And after performing all this work through them, he cast them through death back to the matter to which they belonged, without payment. The Maker, they say, destroyed them. For he took the bodies of Enoch and Elijah up to heaven and promised resurrection in his Scriptures, as he said to Daniel: “Go to the end, rest, and you will rise at your appointed time, at the end of days.” And who indeed compelled Marcion to introduce the subject of matter, unless that matter was his own substance? For what is proclaimed could not fail to disclose its name through the mouths of its proclaimers. And henceforth that matter, which is found among them all, became a sign against them all, so that through one sign against them all it might be known that they too are all one. The weak wild asses, when they see the mighty lion gathering himself, gather against him as though they were mighty and victorious. But he crushes one, and through that one scatters all the many that have gathered together. So too, when truth in its victorious strength defeats one of those who go astray, it also condemns all those [?] who gathered together in that one who was defeated. For all who have gone astray are members of one another. And when a body is caught by one of its members, even the members that were not caught are caught through that one which was caught. For it is written about those earlier deceivers: “All those who came are thieves and robbers.” Blessed is the person who can endure an assault. Blessed too is the person whom their assault has not even reached to disturb him. But what assault is greater than this one from the heretics who say: “Look, good is being purified little by little and ascending.” Oh, what unspeakable madness! For it was not that some further good was being added to the original good, so that the mixture of evil might be diluted and might not overpower the world and choke it. Rather, they resemble fruits whose outward appearance deceives the observer even while they are rotting. But when a fruit is pressed between two strong fingers, it is crushed and the rottenness inside it becomes visible. Let these people too be placed between two sound statements, so that their entire lengthy construction may be dismantled in a short time. For if it is the evil mixed within us, as they say, that harms us, then one of these two things can happen: either that evil must be separated from us so that it does not harm us, or the admixture of good within us must increase, so that the evil within us may be diluted and not kill us.
