The nails bear witness [?] to his death; the angels bear witness to his resurrection. The nails came out of a furnace and became a furnace to confirm us. Their marks proved to Thomas that it was not his soul alone that had risen. Bardaisan demanded that, if these bodies died in Adam, our Lord, who came, ought to raise the body from the [?]. But if it was not the body He revived [?]. Adam brought in the sentence of death for the soul through his sins. The souls that he brought down to Sheol with him, our Lord brought up. [?] his statement at the end. For, he says, our Lord himself said, “Whoever keeps my word will never taste death.” Yet, he says, all who kept it died [?]. Death is sin. For he confused things and began filling a sieve with stones [?] petition. And the statement of [?], whose argument is different, he made the basis of his own argument, in which he explained this death. Souls are held back everywhere, in every depth and dwelling; but those who, he says, have kept our Lord’s word pass out from within the body into the bridal chamber of light. According to the teaching of Bardaisan, the death that Adam introduced was the detention of souls. They were held back at the crossing, for Adam’s sin barred them all. And the life that our Lord introduced, he says, was that he taught the truth and ascended, and brought them across into the kingdom. “Therefore,” he says, “our Lord taught us, ‘Whoever keeps my word will never taste death,’ meaning that his soul is not held back when it passes over the crossing, as in the former detention, when souls were held back before our Savior came.” For him, it is one of two things: [?] someone who kept our Lord’s word died before our Lord. And if the soul did not [?] at the crossing, his soul tasted death. And if he had granted it precedence, [?] what he said about our Lord, that he was the first to cross it. For if Lazarus, when he died, had ascended to the bridal chamber of light, our Lord did him harm by returning him to his body, a prison. And when our Lord himself said to Martha, “Your brother will rise,” from where, then, did he say he would rise—from above or from below? He acted rightly, like a physician, for he uprooted sin, the cause of suffering, from humanity. For the serpent had first bitten Adam, the first man, not with fangs but with advice. He, in turn, healed the wound with commandments, not with medicines. If it was the soul that he came to teach, as they claim, he should have taught the souls in Sheol not to steal or commit adultery. But if souls in Sheol can neither lend nor incur debt, then he came to win victory for both body and soul through his contest and to crown them. He portrayed the example in himself, depicted death in himself, and established a visible demonstration in his body: he triumphed, tasted suffering, and was raised, and clothed himself in glory. He taught that everyone who conducts himself in this way is glorified in this way; whoever fights in this way triumphs, and whoever conquers in this way is crowned. Adam too portrayed in himself an example, so that everyone who sins might look at him: he felt remorse, was exposed, was cursed, went out, was brought low, died, was dissolved, and decayed. He taught that whoever makes wrongdoing his occupation will have remorse as his gain. In both worlds he is mocked; in both worlds he bears disgrace. By the very steps by which Adam had descended, our Lord brought him up. At the beginning he gave him truth in place of the falsehood that the serpent had given him. At the end he gave him life in place of the death that the tree had given. He joined his life to him, half of which was death, to match him [?]. Since, of all the bodies that die, our Lord’s body alone rose, Bardaisan went astray and supposed that it was souls that our Lord raised. He did not consider that Adam’s death also reigned first in Adam himself, and then, after nine hundred years, its leaven spread through all generations. 92. Our Lord too, when he rose, first made life reign in himself, just as death had reigned in Adam. And just as Adam’s death came to reign over everyone after a long time, so too our Lord, after a time, will make his resurrection reign over everyone, so that the destructions may correspond to one another. The leaven of the one who gives life to all has spread throughout the whole mass of the dead, which lies kneaded in the lap of Sheol. For if, after nine hundred years, the leaven of death reigned in us, look, after a little while his living leaven has conquered mortality. And if it is sufficient—as indeed it is sufficient— the argument we have presented concerning the body and its resurrection, the remainder of the discourse that is left will be material for us another day, so that through it, in our discussion, we may trade in the discoveries of our faith. Where he fell, we have stood; where he slipped, we have become firm; and where he [?], we were like him, for we have experienced Adam’s misfortunes: wrongdoing ruled over him at the beginning, and death ruled over him at the end. His body and soul sinned together, but death divided their equality. I thank you, my Master, because you have neither deprived me nor filled me completely. You have not deprived me, so that I may grow; you have not filled me completely, so that I may ask. Someone who is full does not know how to ask; someone who is hungry never stops seeking. You have satisfied me to ease my hunger; you have made me hungry to awaken my prayer.
The discourse against Bardaisan is finished.
A discourse by Saint Ephrem on virginity.

Body, take off that old self, which is entirely hateful, so that it does not wear out the newness that you have entered and put on. For he turns [?] the repayment for his corruption against his garments. If he is renewed, he will in turn wear you out. Body, listen to my advice: take him off through your conduct, so that he does not clothe you in his habits. For look, body, our Lord has made you new through water and rebuilt your old structure—the architect of life, who with his blood fashioned and built himself a temple to dwell in. Do not house that old self in his place in the temple he has renewed. Body, if you let God dwell in your temple, you too will become the palace of his kingdom. Offer his sacrifice as a priest. For nature, which teaches, and Scripture, which proclaims, rebuke this old self. His wickedness is placed between two righteous judges: if he sins without the Law, let his nature rebuke him; and if he sins against the Law, let Scripture rebuke him. Look, he strikes, and they heal. In the wake of wrongdoing they bring repentance, so that through it the sinner may be healed. They scorn the rebel and bind up the repentant. They vindicate judgment, rebuke rebels, and show mercy to penitents and heal them. For they are known to contend with a single evil one who afflicts everyone, who is young in every generation and accompanies everyone and afflicts them at every moment. They too accompany everyone, remain young in every generation, and are present at every moment. Listen to nature and the Law as they recount his evil corruptions. For the people who had the Law committed adultery and fornicated contrary to the Law; the nations changed their nature and acted contrary to their nature. Nature and the law reproached him, because disorder had ruined his order. The lowly slipped away from marriage in the name of discipleship, and when they were caught in between, he placed the shame of failure behind them. And before them stood hateful desire. Because they were ashamed to return to marriage, they fall and are caught in snares. How light your wings are, O virginity! They have grown and risen to where your betrothed sits, at the right hand of the Lord of the heights. Flee from the counsel of the deceitful one, who distributes harm to children. He regularly offers his wares for nothing, to the ruin of the merchants. A cargo of harm impoverished the treasures of great Adam, having traded with his money. Do not borrow from the body, even if it does not demand back what it has lent, for repaying its money brings poverty. For fear, doubt, contempt, and shame accompany its desires. They grieve and distress those who practice them. Only the faces of the chaste, who have stripped it off, are unveiled and pure. Do not be caught, O body, in hateful love. Even when its deed is dead, the thought of it lives on in secret. Subtle and cunning is the discipline that becomes all things to all people, lavishing its gift on the good. He shut the mouths of those who rebuked him with his bread. With a free banquet he bought freeborn people into slavery. He bribed the belly, and it accepted his bribe: the eye was to overlook, the mouth to remain silent, and the ear to make his ugly deeds seem good. His silent wine speaks through those who drink it; it speaks with their voices on its master's behalf. For he is cunning: first he puts food at the mouth of his trap, like a hunter. His love comes before his destruction. Like Judas, who kissed and killed, the Pure One kissed the unclean one, to teach that bitterness and death are secretly mixed into his kisses. This is the one who, if you raise him up, repays you with a fall. When he rises, he makes you think that his desire is dead. And your own flesh gives it life and revives it. When it comes alive in it, it turns and kills it. If you give life to the body's deadness, it in turn will become death to your life. Let fire be an illustration for you: it lies buried and dead in secret, and the rubbing of wood against wood brings it to life, to the destruction of both. Once it comes alive, it turns to burn the very substance that brought it to life by rubbing against it. Oh, what a clear illustration! Wood is made a grave for fire, and when the fire is raised from it, the wood perishes in it. For free will is like life and like a soul to desires, and through it they live. If you cut them off from it and cast them away, they are dead. It has authority: by its will offenses stand. And by its will sins fall. It is the likeness of the Most High, whose power holds everything. And if he withdraws it, everything falls. He is the just judge, who does not call a person to account at the very moment he sins. For this reason conscience comes for two purposes: if a person repents, it covers his wrongdoing; if he rebels, it takes it from him to depart with his spirit. Therefore conscience scrutinizes all our sins, so that it may carry testimony to the court of judgment. Learn repentance, body, and not the remorse that comes at every moment. For repentance is like medicine for our wounds. But this remorse possesses that [?] to build up and tear down pains at every moment. The handwriting on every bond silently accuses the person who owes money. In just the same way, conscience accuses in its silence. It accuses the person who owes a debt of sins. Body, if you become accustomed to repenting and then sinning again, your conscience is the seal on your bond. It is written that if a man falsely accuses his wife, her parents are to bring out and display the evidence of her virginity. Because the judges could not see hidden things, the evidence of virginity on the sheet showed the truth before the judges. But because your betrothed sees hidden things, show your hidden Lord the virginity concealed in your flesh. Show the wrongs done to you not on your sheet but on your body, and show your betrothed your virginity, not on sheets. Cunning Amnon approached the ewe dressed as a lamb. When he had deceived her with what belonged to her, he carried out his own purpose. When he saw that virginity was defiant in her nest, he schemed, brought her into his fold, and then caught her. A healthy wolf, he made himself sick. The sick man then rose to the contest and put on a crown that became his disgrace. He was an athlete who saw that as long as he remained standing, he could not throw his opponent. He hurriedly fell, and then threw her. He broke the yoke through intercourse and rushed into adultery. The wrongdoing he sowed in the chamber he reaped in the wilderness. The sword destroyed him who had destroyed virginity; and he who had stained her with his blood bathed in his own blood. They made him drunk, rose up, and stabbed him. He who had dishonored the ewe was called to account at shearing time. If a virgin is violated in the wilderness, discerning Moses, that advocate of truth, pleads for her: “The girl cried out, but there was no helper.” But who will plead on your behalf, O virginity? For you were taken captive in peacetime and remained silent. Do not surrender yourself to captivity in peacetime, lest peace bring you before the court of judgment. Of the married women and virgins who were in Midian, he killed those who had had sexual relations and spared those who still bore the seal of virginity. If virginity preserved the lives of pagan women, how much more will it give life to chaste women! Look, in the chamber and in the wilderness they lie in wait for you, O virginity. You entered the chamber, and cunning Amnon stole your wealth. You went out into the wilderness, and Shechem the robber plundered your treasure. Where will you go, O enticed dove? For your hunters have multiplied everywhere. Look, O virginity: your hunters, who hunted you, are themselves hunted. They are repaid in reverse: Shechem, who encountered you in the wilderness and took you captive, was slaughtered in his house; and Amnon, in turn, who lay in wait for you in the chamber and took you captive. In the field [?], they violated you and were destroyed. In them a pattern was portrayed: whoever violates you is destroyed. O virgin, innocent dove! Your hunter is cunning, but you are guileless. Your deceiver is skilled, but you are pure. Amnon, under the pretext of food, asked for what he did not want, and through a meal for which he had no hunger, he served his craving for flesh, for which he did hunger. Oh, the deceiver, who asked for something he did not need, so that through this pretext he might gain access to you! For he was asking her for cakes. Oh, the wise woman, who made the cakes a charge against the senseless man! The serpent put on the guise of sickness, so that a hand would make light of him, and then he would strike it. Desire deceived virginity and defiled her. Wrath deceived desire and destroyed him. XXVI. Tamar tore her tunic when she saw that her virginity was lost. She acquired a tunic. Her virginity [?]. She acquired a tunic in place of a tunic. The virginity she had lost was never regained. Craftsmen were able to mend the tears in her clothes. But the damage to her virginity is easy for one alone to heal. O virgin, whom anyone can easily ruin, restoring you is easy only for the Creator of all. Tamar was afraid to remain silent and ashamed to speak. But because she could neither remain silent nor speak, she tore her clothes, so that the visible tears might proclaim the hidden virginity that had been violated. It is a marvel and a wonder that the pearls hanging upon the king’s daughter could not console her for the one she had lost! She was a daughter of kings, whose limbs bore gems and beryls. But virginity alone surpassed them all. Therefore the unclean man scorned the beryls and chose the pearl. He rejected the rings and took away her virginity. The thief knows your value, O virginity, but you have not realized how much you are worth! From among the royal gems he chose and stole a pearl, which left him when he took possession of it. It is a pearl that vanishes from its possessor and does not remain in the thief’s treasury. Innocent Eve encountered the serpent, whose words were bitter and fearsome. She embraced him with love, and he struck her down to destruction. Do not meet with Eve’s fate yourself, lest you find remorse for your soul in it. For if she had shut the door of her hearing against his words, the door of Paradise would not have been shut in her face. Because she gave the evil one’s word room within her mind, the pure garden vomited her out and cast her away. Keep your bosom holy, so that the pure bosom of Paradise may receive you. Do not become dust, the food of the accursed serpent, for dust is his bread, while you are choice salt, which, if it loses its flavor, cannot become fresh salt again. Jephthah’s daughter, who bathed in her blood, was baptized and brought up from it a pearl that uprooted fear and ascended to the treasury on high. The girl who stretched out her neck to be slaughtered by the sword—her consolation was the pure pearl that went with her. But she who loses her virginity here has sorrow as her companion on the day of her departure. At the resurrection, fear becomes her guide. Before the Judge, how bitterly she repents! Jephthah’s daughter chose to die, so that her father’s vow would not be broken. Do not, through your eyes, break the vow of virginity that your mouth has made. Jephthah poured out the blood of his daughter [?]. But as for your own betrothed, his holy blood was poured out for love of you. See, then: the Only Begotten’s blood has purchased the virginal blood with which your gates are sealed, like the gates that were sealed with sprinkled blood in Egypt. For as long as that blood was marked on the outside of the gates, the living within dwelt in peace, as a symbol of virginity. O blood that became a wall for the treasure of life within it! Through it they conquered death. This is the blood that cost them little effort to sprinkle, yet gave them great relief through its protection. Your integrity and your virginity are walls that protect and are protected. When they were protected a little, they protected much. A married woman chose to die so that adultery would be prevented. A virgin died so that a vow would not be broken. If, then, marital union, the mother of offspring, chose to die rather than receive stolen seed whose farmer is accursed, let a virgin not steal impure seed, for even a pure child is wrongdoing within her. Do not, O body, persecute virginity, which has graciously come down to our country and dwells in our land like a foreign guest. If someone persecutes her and tears down her nest, since she cannot return and rebuild it, her wings quickly carry her up on high. She is a bird of the heights that grows old in a single nest, and if she departs, she leaves it forever. When the friendship of the Watchers flies away, the companionship of demons enters in its place. Desire, which is virginity’s adversary, was driven by Joseph from his body, so that it would not dwell in him. The friendship of the Watchers flees away with the Watchers. Who would not weep that, in place of that peaceful one, a tormenting one has entered and settled there? Let youth fear wine, which overpowered Lot in his old age. If wine accomplished the difficult deed of enabling women to steal pregnancy through it, how much more will it accomplish the easy deed of enabling men to steal virginity through it! Young girls plundered the old man’s treasures. You, guard your treasury against young men! XL. Fear wine as well. For it exposed the honored Noah. He who had overcome the flood of water was overcome by a handful of wine. The flood outside him could not overpower him, but the wine inside him quietly robbed him. If wine exposed and brought down Noah, the ancestor of peoples and languages, how much more has it overcome you, who have been bribed! Do not trust wine, for it is a false god and a troublemaker that hands over your fortress, so that a captor may come and carry your freedom off into slavery, and your love may follow his will. And when you have utterly lost your true betrothed and acquired a false one in his place, what consolation will you have in saying, “Even though I have lost, yet I have found”? For his love is lying and deceitful, bestowed on everyone. He will not stay with you, and then the soul will have many regrets. Then you will be hemmed in on either side and deprived on both sides. The faithful one has abandoned you because you abandoned him, and the false companion whom you loved has deserted you and left you at the crossroads. Where, then, will you turn your gaze, innocent dove who tore up her nest and went out after a serpent in her love? Your pearl is a pearl that flies away from between two sides and is lost. For only chaste merchants can possess it, and if they become defiled, both lose it. O pearl, greater than everything! Yet the fool hands the pearl over to the thief with his own hands. The person drunk on wine is better off than the one drunk on vile love. For counsel and instruction given under compulsion are dreams to him, and a beating is as though it were no beating. Tight shackles are loose to him; the staff is contemptible, the club weak, and the rod despised. Correction is a story to him, and rebuke passes through his ears like a tale. Disgrace is like entertainment, and spittle on his face is like dew. For the path of the words that strike his ears does not lead to his heart. The gates of his ears stand open opposite one another. A word that enters one ear goes straight out through the other. All the words poured into it he channels outside. His teacher thinks that the instruction is entering, but does not realize that all of it is flowing out and spilling away, because there is no room in his mind to receive it. For the recesses of his thoughts are full, crowded, and blocked up, from the little drop of evil love that dripped into him and became a great sea. And there his thoughts sink and struggle like sailors whose ships have been wrecked. There his mind lies polluted, like a ship without a sailor. And when the law, like a sailor, wishes to bring it to a good harbor, it fights against its sailor. It is its own ruin that it loves. O youth, mistress of races, do not finish your race in the turmoil of lusts. When he has worked in you and taken your strength, he quickly abandons you, so that your old age becomes a laughingstock: you have kept a hateful course in store for it, to its disgrace. Hasten your race in the contest, O youth, so that you may set a crown upon your old age. For when old age grows dull and its understanding diminishes, people remember the modesty of its youth. When it has gathered up his understanding, those who see the defects of his body recoil from it. But those who see its hidden spiritual plantings cherish him. Inscribe your victories upon your limbs, O youth, so that through them you may be honored when you grow old. Inscribe all your acts of charity upon your hands. Mark your footsteps with visits to the sick; paint the image of your Lord upon your heart. And if mounted panels, assembled by a carpenter and painted by a painter, are hailed and even bowed down to because of the royal image, how much more, then, will your limbs be honored, upon which the images of your King are painted! 52. Youth is like a branch bearing good fruit, beautiful in summer; but when its fruit and leaves have been stripped away, it becomes ugly. Everyone turns their face away from it, and what was desired above all becomes despised by all. Young girl, do not display your beauty to outsiders, for when it becomes ugly and grows old, those who see it despise it. O eye, do not let the beauty of youth take you captive, for the blemishes of old age lie hidden within it. For the limbs of youth, beautiful to look at, carry those blemishes, but old age exposes them. For a borrowed beauty rested upon them; even while it was dwelling and settled there, it departed and flew away. But if captivity at the hands of kings should confront you, and they expose your modesty in the wilderness, the very defiling coercion of captivity testifies on your behalf that you are holy, just as Sarah remained holy in the unclean embrace of the defiled Pharaoh. For her heart did not [?] of its own free will. Her will served as priest for her body, and with its hyssop washed the body that had been defiled by force. For just as a priest can purify the temple in which he ministers, so a pure will can purify the body, the temple within which it serves as priest. For a human being is a marvel: although he is one, he is his own temple and his own priest. He is his own sacrificial priest and his own sacrifice. He is the offering, and he is the one who presents the offering. For he resembles that Lamb of God, who was himself everything for himself.
The discourse on virginity is finished.

Another discourse against Mani. Let Mani be questioned about that ruler: if he belongs to the evil portion—that is, to the being that loves adultery, as they say— why did he say, “You shall not commit adultery,” and the rest? Know that he commanded the very thing he chose for himself. And look: it was because of sins that he completely uprooted the Hebrews. And [?] and [?] that he is mixed. Let him divide a portion, and he should not have commanded [?] from the hearer [?] a hateful commandment [?] of them all. How did he say, “There is none besides me,” and how, again, did he kill Jesus? And if these people were drunk, they would not refrain, not even if he had commanded them. So he did indeed gratify the sinners with a command to sin. For if they committed adultery even when he said, “Do not commit adultery,” how much more would they have done so if he had commanded them to commit adultery! But if he loved good things and commanded them, let them say who was undoing his commandments so that they would not be fulfilled. If Satan was undoing them, then both of them are from one evil essence, as they say. And how does half of it fight by means of good, and half of it by means of evil? But if he became good because the admixture of good was abundant in him, then the Good One himself is evil, because he did not further increase another power in them. Then the evil, like the good, would have been children of his own nature. Why, then, did that ruler not accept the good Jesus? For, as they say, there is an opportunity for good to be mixed with him and accepted by him. For if it is mixed with him, it is accepted by him. Indeed, when Jesus came, he was mixing his good words. Why did he not mix good portions into them? But if he does not accept even the good words that are mixed into him, then neither can he accept the portion. For just as his evil hearing is foreign to the good word, so his hateful essence is foreign to the beautiful portion. For if the evil willingly accept the mixing of portions, how is it that they did not accept the mixing of words? And if the portions are mixed into them by force, why does the Good One look for their consent for words to be mixed into them? But observe that deadly evil is present in fruits, in seed, and in springs. Yet it is good that gives life [?] through them to human beings. How does evil overcome good, seeing that good itself is present in abundance? And if [?] was confined, but because of [?] bound [?] henceforth, and ceased from [?]. And if the mixture Look, or why not [?] who [?] of the lamb? Or if that victorious one is in the lamb [?], or if in the lamb’s body it was dormant and quiet and in the body of wolves it was [?], then evil comes from the body and not from [?]. And if he wished, then [?] and fashioned for matter a lamb’s body. That [?] innocent [?] good [?] let evil bodies be fashioned for it [?] and that which is evil and hateful in the animal; yet the Being is good in that he exists, and [?] those [?] who exist, so that they may exist. He preserved his own likeness [?]. He too exists, and those who exist he destroys without darkness. An adversary [?] made. For he ought to have done to himself the very same thing that he did to another. But say that the Maker too did it first, they say, to [?] before passing on to another. But let them know that the Maker, in what he made [?], is found in this greatness, and not the Being toward [?] where this nature is found, which he gave it when he created it [?]. That is, that he should preserve himself and destroy others—he is the Being, if he is a Being. How can it produce something whose character is not present in its being and nature, out of anything within it? For it fled [?], and an opposing agency becomes necessary. But since this too is good, both in its activity and toward what it has made, it is not hostile. [?] the maker in it, and what is made also rejoices in it. That is, God and man. Thus both the destroyer and the one destroyed would be distressed by that destruction, apart from the matters prescribed in the establishment of the law, on the condition that the disciplinarian finds satisfaction in them and the offender is distressed by them. But just as there is no suffering when that offender agrees with the disciplinarian's will, so, when the one being destroyed comes to agree with the destroyer's will, there will be no destruction. And just as the disciplinarian's will was not that he should suffer, so too will the destroyer's will be—that is, not to cause pain. For a just self-existent being, just as it is by nature in itself, is also by nature toward another. The reverse of this, then, ought to be found in an unjust self-existent being. For a just self-existent being destroys neither itself nor others. As for an unjust self-existent being, who is this that protects itself like a just one, but acts unjustly toward someone who has not wronged it? This very fact, along with many others and more than many others, testifies against it that it is not a self-existent being, but a composite. And if they say that the children of darkness are divided against one another, then the very same thing that is said about all of them is also said about each one of them individually. That is, each one of them is divided against its own members, just as it is also divided against its companions. For if there is harmony within each one of them, it ought to be found among them all; and the same applies to division. And if they are fighting among themselves and do not cease fighting one another, how did they come to wage war against the luminous one? For look, they have that very opponent from among themselves and within themselves. Either he is a relative of the luminous one, opposed to them, or he is a third being who has become an opponent of both. For he must give him a place and existence, from himself and for him. Then there is opposition even within that nature of the luminous one. But if there is none within it because it is one nature, then what I said above has been confirmed: that division exists because two natures are mingled with one another, as the body and soul also testify. But which of the natures is more abundant, Mani: darkness or the luminous one? If darkness were more abundant, it could not have been defeated by the luminous one. And if the children of darkness are killed, as they say, why are they not all killed, if their nature is mortal? And if in the end he is indeed imprisoned because he does not die, then he stands convicted of having lied about their death. And why do the natures hate one another? For look, the body and soul that came from him love one another. And if this is because one has mingled with the other—for mingling can indeed change our nature—then, since, look, it has changed in body and soul, and with [?] the two of them have one nature, a nature that does not [?]. Let them say of the mixture what they said of the soul: it absolves them, and that it is not like [?]. And if fire mingled with fire, water with water, and wind with wind, necessarily light also mingled with light. All sensible people, apart from madmen, know that these substances are related to one another. Perhaps even madmen know it, apart from the Manichaeans. For we know the causes through which water is transformed, and we testify unanimously to this: look, in a tree it is transformed into wine, oil, and its many flavors. What, then, shall we say? That wine is not related to water, or that oil, too, does not belong to its kind? And if wine and oil, which are indeed very different from water, are not foreign to it, even though they appear foreign, how much more closely related must water be to water, even if it is bitter! For just as water is transformed in plants, so it is also transformed in different soils, while it and the soils and the plants are under one will, that of the Creator of all. For if they were being purified, this would also be perceptible, because the fire would have become weaker than it is, owing to the purification of that other fire which separated from it. For there are old people who have lived more than a hundred years, and they have not noticed that this fire, after a hundred years, is cold or weak, nor that the fire of a hundred years ago was hotter, stronger, brighter, or clearer than this fire. For these substances, which have not grown weak and are not growing weak, themselves demonstrate against Bardaisan and Mani that their teaching has no substance. But if something pushed it from behind and drove the element of wind, as Bardaisan said, it would have driven it toward its diametrical opposite. And because they are particles, as Bardaisan said, an individual one of them can be distinguished only in thought, it is clear that the beings did not push one another as bodies push bodies. From them and through them, one can establish that wind cannot move the light of the sun. Or let us state the truth: this fire does not come from that fire of which Bardaisan spoke. But there is no possibility that a creation like this could come from those self-existent beings of which Bardaisan himself spoke. For their natures, bound to their essential existence, do not allow them to be fashioned as the craftsman requires. For a creation from nothing—he created and established it in whatever manner and to whatever extent pleased the Maker. He changes and transforms it; he dissolves it and also gives it light. But if they are particles of self-existent substance, as they say, which cannot be dissolved, but can be gathered together, let them explain to anyone who wishes to ask without disputing how things of an uncompounded nature can be compounded unless the fixed structure of their essential existence—that is, their particles—is dissolved. But if they were scattered abroad, they are gathered together by wisdom and compressed through exertion. And now let us say to him what Bardaisan himself said to someone else: And if the fabric of the essential existence of these particles is woven together and closely packed [?] This, however, is the fabrication: that by their nature they can be gathered together through wisdom and joined together through craftsmanship. And if this is the whole of its creative activity, it is a feeble [?], since its action extended only as far as gathering them together. But if creation too was created from these atoms, I want to learn how, when one atom joined another, a soul came into being, and when another joined another, a body came into being. What is the glue and cement that holds them together so that they do not come apart? If the binding itself also consists of atoms, then the binding itself still needs another binding to bind it. For a rope made of sand cannot bind grains of sand into a single body, because it cannot even hold itself together or bind its own substance. For copper that is smelted from sand, however firmly you press its particles against one another, increases and becomes a large heap of sand. That is, they do not stick to one another unless they enter the furnace and are released by fire, one by one, from the bonds of their nature. When the fixed structure of each one is dissolved, then they all become a single mixture in the crucible, and a single force binds them together. It is like stones: unless they are dissolved and become [?], they cannot be worked together and become a single mass of copper. If, then, each of these atoms of the self-existent entities can also be smelted, and their substance can be destroyed, although it was not fashioned, and their nature dissolved, although it is not composite, they have admitted against their will that these were not self-existent entities but things that were made, nor natures bound to existence, but natures fashioned by creative activity. And creation was not from something, but from nothing. And even if we concede to them what truth never concedes to falsehood, namely, that creation came or comes into being from atoms, how did knowledge and thought come, or how do they come, into being from atoms? But there are some among their secret sages who twist things in order to say something subtle: there are, they say, other atoms belonging to mind, power, and thought—that is, belonging to three other self-existent entities, which were sent by the Lord of all against the primeval darkness and for this formation. And from these atoms, they say, a mixture was made, and they are mixed with these other ones, as Bardaisan said: the power of the first utterance that remained in creation did everything [?] of our soul. But if this blasphemy cannot be believed, then, according to his premise, knowledge has been found to be no less than God, nor even like heat from fire. For if that were so, it would necessarily follow that, just as the heat of fire is not divided in its action toward water and toward itself, Thus even our ignorance concerning God would have been divided. If it had been from him, from God. But since it is not from God, nor indeed from the self-existent Being himself, it is certain that the whole human being was created from nothing. And this one thing bears witness concerning everything, that it too was created from nothing. But you should know that, as far as these matters gave Bardaisan a helping hand, he dragged them along after his own will. But where he lost track of them and they became hidden from him, he too drifted about in bewilderment. For he claimed that the names of the months were not assigned without a purpose, but symbolically. He began with the first Tishri, saying that this month, by its name, proclaims the name of the first beginning. To avoid making this too long for us, let us say briefly that he went on interpreting the names of the months as far as Nisan. But when he came to the name of Nisan and saw that its name did not suit his interpretation, nor did those of the five other months after it, he interpreted up to that point and stopped. He explained as far as Adar and ceased. But if mysteries had been placed by God in the names of the months, he would have depicted mysteries and symbols in the names of all the months of the year. For look: Nisan, which is greater than all the others, has a name that does not correspond to its event—that is, its name does not correspond to the salvation that took place in it. So, because some names corresponded to the months—those that happened to correspond by chance— he gathered an explanation from them, pieced it together, and made an interpretation out of them. He drew from the language of Beth Garmai and from the language of Edessa, and traveled around sea and land to make one convert. And see how the fruit is at odds with its root: his son disagreed with his interpretation. For Bardaisan said and explained that the first month was called Tishri as though prophetically, and the one after it Marheshvan, because, he said, all things stir in it. He did not say “Tishri and Tishri.” His son, however, in order to establish another mystery that he was putting together, and also so that pure lips could speak it and chaste ears hear it, did not say “Tishri and Marheshvan,” but “Tishri and Tishri.” For he said this in his hymn: “O Tishri, mother of the year, give birth for us to another Tishri.” He said this about the Mother of Life, when he asked her to give birth and leave a daughter in her likeness. Bardaisan also spoke in this way about the self-existent beings and their colors. For he said that light is white, fire red, wind blue, and water green. He had stolen these things from the Greeks. Just as he explained that each of them has its own color, so each of them has its own smell, its own taste, its own texture, and its own sound. For each of the self-existent beings must possess five properties, corresponding to the five senses we have. As he himself said, “Everything that exists has its own power, its own color, and its own form, and the rest of whatever belongs to it.” Let him show us, then, what light feels like to the touch, and what wind tastes like, and what fire smells like, so that you may know that here too, in dealing with the natures, he proceeds just as he did with the names of the months. He displayed some of them as though to demonstrate his philosophy. But when other aspects of them sank away from him and were hidden, he began to float about; and when he sank, to no avail, and failed to master them, he neglected the matter, passed on, and began something else. He deceived his listeners into supposing that he also knew those other things that had not been discussed, just as he knew their counterparts that had been discussed. So too he places darkness below them all because of its weight. And if darkness is heavy, understand that water, being lighter, must therefore be above it in its own region. And because fire in turn is lighter than water, it must also be above water. And because wind, in turn, is lighter than fire, it is clear that it too is above fire. And because light is lighter than wind, it is evident that it is above wind. For each one of them is lighter than the heavy substance below it, but heavier than the light substance above it. By this straightforward comparison and fair weighing, the element of water is found between darkness and fire: one cold, below it, and the other hot, above it. And the philosopher’s construction is left in ruins. For if wind struck the fire below it and pushed it downward toward darkness, the fire would not reach it, because the great element of water stands between it and darkness. Thus the intervening extinguisher would not allow the thing that stirs up darkness to rub against it, so that its smoke might billow up and reach its neighbor. For it necessarily follows, if the natures of the primordial beings truly correspond to their names—if fire really is fire and not an empty name— that water too is truly water. And if it is water, it is the opposite of fire. It would therefore not allow fire to approach darkness. And because water was darkness’s neighbor, cold was added to cold for darkness. This is the opposite of the story they fabricated: “Heat dissolved its cold, and its smoke billowed up.” But if it had billowed up and risen, since they stand one above another, as their light and heavy natures teach us, it was not merely the lower extremity of them all that was destroyed, as Bardaisan said. For how can heavy and light substances stand equally at one level or within one region? The pans of a balance demonstrate this, as do water and oil placed in a vessel: the lighter substance stays above and the heavier below. Thus, when darkness sought to rise and reach the heels and lower edges of the light above, in its attempt to rise it completely covered water, fire, and wind. Yet only the lower extremity of light was destroyed! Thus they have been refuted, and Bardaisan’s followers can no longer fabricate stories as though they came from him.
